FLINT (Yarmouth) moved that the fourth report of the Joint Committee on the Printing of Parliament be concurred in.
Mr. CHARLES MARCIL (Bonaventure) moved in amendment :
That after the words 1 Civil Service Act ' at the close of the third paragraph of the report, the fallowing words be added : * And that the salaries of the said officials be continu:d as at present, notwithstanding anything fo the contrary in the aforesaid Act.'
He said : I am requested by the chairman of the Printing Committee, who is unavoidably absent, to explain that the object of this amendment is to cover the case of three clerks who are at present employed in the Printing Bureau, in the distribution office, and who have been up to this time under the control of the committee. By the report of the committee, they are to be placed under the control of the Secretary of State, and to come within the purview of the Civil Service Act. The amendment is to meet any objections which may be raised by the Auditor General to the payment of their salaries.

LaRIVIERE (Provencher). Do I understand that by this resolution these officers will be debarred from any increase if they were held to be otherwise entitled to it ? I can understand the object or the motion in providing that the salaries shall not be decreased, but I do not think the officers should be deprived of their title to an increase if the committee should recommend it and the government grant it.

I think the object of this resolution is to assure these officers of their present salaries in the transfer from one branch to the other. I do not think it would have the effect of preventing an increase, but that will have to be looked into. Of course, there can be no intention of interfering with these officers getting any reasonable and proper increase that they would otherwise receive.
Amendment agreed to ; and motion, as amended, agreed to.

speechtext:
In moving the adoption of the second report of the Joint Committee on the Library of Parliament, I am desired by the committee

to bring to the particular attention of the House one feature of that report, which is the following : It was ordered, in the interest of the library, and for the greater convenience of the members, that rule 118 of the House be strictly carried out. That rule provides :
At the first meeting of the Joint Library Committee at every session of parliament the librarian shall report a list of the books absent at the commencement of the session, specifying the names of any persons who have retained the same in contravention of either of the foregoing rules.
As a matter of fact, this particular rule, as well as other rules framed for the government of the library, in the past, have been more honoured in the breach than the observance. The committee have discovered that irregularities on the part of members of parliament in relation to the library are not at all infrequent. The chief irregularities may be stated as follows : Want of promptness in returning new books during the session of the House ; keeping useful books that are not new for an undue period ; taking out books by members for strangers, and mailing the same all over the country ; and retaining of books of reference during many weeks of the session, this being directly contrary to the specific rule. The fact is, that at the present time, a very large number of books which should be in the library are not there, and a very considerable number of books that were owned by the library, and that should be there, have been lost, and a considerable expenditure has to be entailed in buying again these particular books. But the most serious phase of the matter is that books which are required during the session by members are not to be found in the library. Just to show the House the extent to which some of these irregularities have been carried, let me give a list of the number of books not returned by ex-members of parliament and present members. I may say that this is by no means a complete list. The committee were informed that one ex-member of the House had twelve books away from the library, contrary to rules ; another had 17, another 6, another 20, another 11, another 9, another 11, another 39, another 13, another 14, and still another 39. making an average of 19 books to each of this list of twelve ex-members. All of these books have been out of the library for years and are in reality lost to the library. Taking the present members of parliament, one has 7 books out, another 11, another 13, another 10, another 5, another 7, another 22, another 20, another 18, another 7, and still another 7. Thus twelve members have an aggregate of 135 books out, or an average of 11 each. These books have been out of the library in each case more than a year. The Library Committee have thought proper to bring this matter directly to the attention of the House, 1401
and to give the House specific and distinct notice that the rule which I have read, and which is to be found in the rules of the House of Commons, shall next year be strictly enforced. The librarian will be required to furnish a list at the first meeting of the committee next session, and steps will be taken to give the list of delinquents such publication as may then be deemed to be, in the interests of the library and the members of this House, necessary and advisable.

I, am not going to say anything in opposition to the report or the suggestions contained In it, because I think they are in the right direction. I want to refer to what has been the experience of some members in the past, which may result in an injustice being done them. Sometimes reports are sent out from the library that books are held by members although these books were returned during the session. Either through accident or carelessness these books when returned were not credited to the members against whom they were charged. I know that that has been my own case several times. I know of cases in which the books were never taken out of the House of Commons but simply used in the House and then sent back and not credited. Then sometimes the books may be mislaid in the library and it is not known to the members who returned them whether they were credited to them or not. In many instances there are mistakes of that character, which do a great injustice to members who remain charged with books which were returned.
Motion agreed to.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to inquire of the government whether a report that a detachment of (troops will be called out on the 24th of Slay for drill and march into the country on the Sabbath, 25tli of May, some five miles from the city and camp there, is correct or not ? I heard this matter alluded to yesterday in some of the Sunday pulpits. If any intention of that kind exists, I beg to bring the matter to the attention of the government and ask the reconsideration of the order, if It has been made. Such a step) would antagonize the sentiment of a very large portion of the inhabitants of Canada, and as this is a Christian nation and we profess some regard for Sabbath observance, I rise to request that consideration be given to the question.

Unfortunately, my hon. colleague the Minister of Militia is not here at the moment and I cannot answer for him as I know nothing about the matter, but I will call the attention of my hon. colleague to it when he comes.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sit Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: There is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the bon. Minister of Militia and I take this opportunity of doing so, although he is not here at present, in order that it may be brought to his notice when here. I believe that the House understood, from the explanation given by that hon. Minister, some weeks ago, that the Coronation contingent was to be thoroughly representative of the active militia, mounted police and the various contingents which have served in South Africa. Recently I have been given to understand that the representation would be confined to the members of the active militia and mounted police force and Strath-cona Horse. If that report is correct it leaves out the members of the second contingent, the first mounted rifles, the Royal Canadian Dragoons, and the Canadian Artillery. In case the rumour is correct, I would like to say that the second contingent was certainly the most thoroughly representative contingent that went to the front. It was drawn from all parts of Canada and it was the only one that was so drawn. The first contingent did not include any representatives from the North-west. The Strathcona Horse came entirely from the west, but the second contingent was drafted from all parts of Canada, and I should think that that contingent Is entitled to representation at the Coronation as well as the others mentioned.
GALVHEATJ (Temiscouata) moved that the House go into committee on Bill (No. 102) to incorporate the GaspS and Western; Railway Company.

Because there are two companies, it must he specific :
Of the company interested and of the bondholders thereof.
Now again it goes on and says :
At which meeting shareholders representing at least two-thirds in value of the stock are present or represented by proxy.
I propose to add after the word ' shareholders ' 'of the company interested and of the bondholders thereof ' holding at least two-thirds of the bonds. I think the House will see this is a fair proposition, and that there can be no serious objection to putting this in so as to protect the bondholders if the Bill is to pass, to protect them effectively against anything that may be done against their interests, either by the Baie des Chaleurs Railway Company or by the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company, or the directors thereof. Also :
3. By erasing the words 'and no prescription or statute of limitation should be urged against the payment of said claims by the company, and no valid title shall pass to the company until said claims have been paid to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council.
Now, as to the first part of this amendment, I want to draw attention to the fact that the Bill as amended provides not only for a voluntary sale or lease of the railway, but also for the sale by authority of justice,
by sheriff's sale. In the latter case prescription has been running against a great many of these claims-which it has been stated amount to about $70,000 or more. The prescription has been running under the law of Quebec, under the Civil Code of Quebec ; and this law practically amends the Civil Code of Quebec to the extent that it does away with the prescription, which, under our code, in these cases of wage earners and of boarding housekeepers and hotelkeepers, is acquired by two years. This is done away with, this law amends the civil law of the province of Quebec to that extent. I point out to the House that I do not think any private railway company coming before this House with such an amendment to the civil law of Quebec, can expect their request to be adopted. I call the attention of those who are responsible for the legislation in this House to that very serious question. If it can be done upon this private Bill, upon this measure which is to incorporate a private company for the building of a. railway, it can be done on any other measure that comes before this House. It is a bad precedent to which I call the attention of the law officers of the Crown. As to the second part of the amendment, it is explained by the amendment which I will move in a short time, that is, as to the payment of the claims. I have provided for that by another section. The section as it stands now simply provides that the company shall pay the claims, and that no title shall vest in the company until the claims have been paid to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council. I have substituted another clause, which I think will meet with the approval of the promoters of the Bill, and particularly of those who are interested in the payment of the claims which are provided for by this Bill. To subsection 4 there were added the following words :
But nothing in this section shall in any way affect the rights of the bondholders of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company and of the Baie des Chaleurs Railway Company*
I propose to substitute for that the following saving clause :
Provided that nothing in this Act shall in any way affect the rights of the bondholders of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company and of the Baie Des Chaleurs Railway Company.
The House will see that I have substituted for the word ' section ' in this saving clause, the word ' Act.' Now, it may be said that the rights of the bondholders are sufficiently protected. I do not see it in that light. When the credit of the country is involved all due regard should be given to the rights of the creditors, and every precaution taken to save their rights would be a saving also of the credit of the country. If it can be said that by legislation the rights of the bondholders who have ad-

vanced their money for a railway enterprise such as this can be wiped out, if the security which this country generally offers for such advances in money, can be wiped out, the credit of the country will be diminished to that extent. Then I also propose that the following should be added to section 9 of the Bill :
No valid title shall pass to. the company until the said company shall have deposited in the hands ot the hon. Minister ol Railways and Canals the sum of $100,000 in cash, to be used and employed by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals to pay the overdue balances in settlement of the claims mentioned in subsection 4 of the next preceding section. Upon and after the depositing by the company of the said sum1, the Minister of Railways and Canals shall appoint a commissioner, who, after investigation, shall pay to the creditors and claimants the said claims, or so much thereof as may be due, and the remuneration or salary of the said commissioner shall be paid out of the said deposit ; the balance of which, if any after deducting the amount paid out, and the said remuneration or salary, shall be refunded to the company.
The Bill provides for the payment of outstanding balances due for labour, board and materials supplied and furnished for the construction and operation of the railway. These bondholders took possession of the railway in July, 1900, and no claims are now outstanding for the operation and maintenance of the railway against the bondholders ; and a thing which has been unheard of in connection with this railway is that ever since the bondholders have been in possession the railway has been operated to the general satisfaction of the community, and there is not one farthing due for anything in connection with the railway, for supplies, work or board bills, or anything like that. I hold in my hand a copy of a certificate given by the controller of the Post Office Department, in which he says that the mail service has been carried on entirely since July, 1900. This shows that the bondholders are acting in good faith, that they are doing what they are bound to do in carrying out their obligations towards the country. The Bill as passed by the Bailway Committee provides, as I have said, for the payment of the outstanding balances due by company before the bondholders took possession of the road. It is said that no title shall pass to the company until these balances have been paid to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council, but I will call the attention of the House to the fact that it will be in the interest and to the advantage of the company to get these claims settled for as littlte money as possible, and that this has already been done in connection with this very same railway. They were forced under the law of Quebec to pay these outstanding balances and claims, and people have been fleeced because the company, naturally, has every interest in paying as little Mr. CASGRAIN.
as possible of these outstanding balances, and in getting rid of them for as little money as they can take out of their pockets. I call the attention of the government and of hon. members who are specially interested, and particularly the hon. member for Bona-venture (Mr. Marcil), that if the amendment which I propose is adopted, then there can be no such dealing with these people : they will be paid every cent which is due them. I propose that a deposit shall be made with tiie hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, that a commissioner shall be appointed by him to pay these claims, and that it is only-on his report, after he has made an investigation, that these claims have been paid by the company, that the title shall pass. It seems to me that this is an amendment which should commend itself to those who are interested in the payment of these claims before the company takes possession of the road. I have a precedent for this. Some time in 1889, or 1890, a certain part of a subsidy which had been voted by the provincial House, amounting to $28,000, which was due in claims, was to be paid by the government of the province of Quebec, and a commissioner was appointed by the then government, who went up there, paid all the claims, or paid part of the claims to the extent of $28,000 which were outstanding at that time. It seems to me that this is an amendment which should fairly commend itself to those who are really interested in seeing that these people shall be paid. I would ask that when this Bill is sent back to the Railway Committee, these amendments be made to it.

Mr. Speaker, when this Bill was under consideration by the Railway Committee the disposition of the committee, as I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) will allow, was to see that in every respect the rights of the existing bondholders, and of every existing creditor having claims upon it, were recognized and protected in the fullest degree. It was tiie endeavour of the committee to attain that end, and when the amendments had been made the hon. gentleman who has now given notice of some amendments to the Bill as reported was asked if they were satisfactory to him, or if he had any suggestions to make, in order to still further secure and protect the rights of the people he represents. The hon. gentleman, at that time, was not able to offer any further proposition, and the Bill therefore went through.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Biair).

speechtext: I said then that I could not, at the moment, on an important Bill of this kind, say that these amendments were satisfactory. When the Bill was passed, I said that I reserved my right to offer any other amendment, which after due consideration I thought should be made. That was the understanding.

Quite so. 1 do not think I have misstated the hon. gentleman's position. I say the hon. gentleman was not then able to make any further suggestion. I do not say that it is not proper for him to make the suggestion which he has made now, but I want to dispel any impression that the hon. gentleman's remarks may have left upon the House, that the committee were in the slightest degree indisposed to adopt any amendment necessary to secure the rights of the parties he represents. That was the feeling and desire on the part of the committee. I think myself that the hon. gentleman is quite within his right and is quite* free, notwithstanding anything that occurred before the committee, to suggest whatever he may regard as important tu further protection to these rights. It may well be that lie might fairly expect that some of his clauses should be adopted by the House. In the first place he wants to have inserted the word 'bondholders,' meaning that the bondholders should be consulted as well as the shareholders of the company in order that the concurrence of a proper proportion ot them should be had before any agreement should take effect for the transfer of this company to the present company. That is not an unreasonable proposition. It may be that it would be a little cumbrous to give to the shareholders who, the hon. gentleman says, have been superseded by the bondholders the same voting power, but I do not see at the moment how you could very well set aside the shareholders, and ns 1 am at present advised I would be disposed to think that it would be proper to add the bondholders, leaving the shareholders their present rights in that respect. As one member of the committee, I would vote for that, so that the bondholders may be able to protect themselves in as much ns they have superseded the shareholders, and in ns much by legislation of this parliament they have been placed practically in control of one of the railways at least.
I do not think that the third clause is as clear as the hon. gentleman assumes it to be. He would urge that no prescription or statutory limitation should be urged against the payment of claims by the company. He thinks it improper to insert that clause in the Bill, and he further contends that it is beyond our constitutional powers, because in his opinion we would thereby be amending the Civil Code of the province of Quebec. 1 may be wrong in the hasty conclusion I have arrived at on that point, but I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman. We are simply providing here as respects certain claims which are mentioned in this section ; which are not the claims of the bondholders or of those who hold securities and have priority on the property of the company. but which are claims enumerated in the Bill and which are mentioned ns claims for labour, the boarding house claims,
material and supplies furnished for the construction and operation of the railway. Those claims are being dealt with not as a matter of legal right, but we are simply recognizing that it would be proper to attach as a condition of the transfer of these railway properties, after the prior securities have been dealt with and before this company shall take over this railway property either at judicial sale or by agreement, that the particular claimants named here shall be paid in full disregarding any prescription which might militate against their recovery in law. Wo attach that as a condition to the transfer of the property. We are not interfering at all with anybody's legal rights, and we do not profess to interfere with the Civil Code of Quebec. We simply impose a condition upon the transfer of this property and if that condition is too onerous the company need not comply with it. If they are willing to take the transfer under this condition, they can do so, but if they are not willing they need not do so. I cannot agree that my hon. friend is right in asking that we should say that the company which takes over this property, shall only be asked to pay what claims are not barred. That would be the effect of his amendment if we adopted it. I would therefore think that clause 3 of the amendment should not pass.
I see no objection to clause 4 of the amendment, but I think it unnecessary, because the only section of the whole Bill which attempts to deal with the rights of creditors, mortgagees, or others is the ninth section. However, if the hon. gentleman thinks that his position and that of this clients would be any stronger. I would not hesitate to change the word ' section ' into the word ' act.'
The 5th clause of the amendment is :
That no valid title shall pass to the company until the said company shall have deposited in the hands of the Minister of Railways the sum of $100,000 in cash.
I think that is unnecessary. My hon. friend has no concern at all with regard !o the claimants who are referred to in the last section ; he is particularly concerned -on behalf of the bondholders, and if there is any conflict of interest, that conflict would be between the bondholders whom he represents and these claimants whom he does not represent.
speakername: Tlie MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I beg the bon. gentleman's pardon ; I am here to legislate and make good law.

I do not at all wish to make any disagreeable reference to my hon. friend in the matter, but I rather understood him before the committee to say, that he was speaking for the bondholders and acting for them, which I thought lie might properly do. Did I not correctly understand that ?

Mr. CASGRA1N. Certainly, tout that does not preclude me from amending the Bill in any proper interest when it comes before the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I perfectly understand that, tout I rather drew the inference that as the hon. gentleman was representing the interests of the bondholders in a professional way outside of his toeing a member of parliament- and perhaps before he was a member of parliament-I could not help thinking that liis interest as representing the bondholders would be rather in conflict with the interest of the other claimants. However, I do not know that is germane to the question, and I shall not dwell on it. If those who are anxious for the right of these claimants referred to in the latter portion of the section, have thought it necessary to seek this provision. They are content that it should be left with the Governor in Council, the Minister of Railways or the Railway Committee to ascertain just what claims there are outstanding. By the usual methods-public advertisement. I presume, they would Jnvite anybody and everybody who had such claims to send them to the department. Then the department would examine into them, and endeavour to adjust them, and having ascertained the gross amount of claims, the duty would necessarily devolve upon one or other branch of the government to see that the claims were fully paid before a declaration should be made to the effect that they had been paid, and before a valid title could pass to this company. Therefore, I do not think it would be necessary to adopt the fifth clause of my hon. friend's amendment. My hon. friend from Terrebonne (Mr. Prefon-taine) has an amendment which he thinks of proposing to my hon. friend's fourth amending clause, and which is a little more specific than anything contained in the Bill, and to which he (Mr. Casgrain) might perhaps give his assent. But, with the exception of the third and fifth clauses, I can see no objection to my hon. friend's amendment being adopted by the House. Do I understand the motion of my hon. friend to be to refer the Bill back to the Railway Committee ?- because he has given notice to refer it to the committee of the whole House. We cannot refer it back to the Railway Committee now; but if he will accept the suggestion I make, we might refer it to the committee of the whole House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In view of the statement of the hon. minister, I will not insist on that portion of the motion, to refer the Bill back to the Railway Committee. I understand that the hon. minister does not object to three of the amendments I propose. Of course, when the Bill goes to the Committee of the Whole. I presume these amendments will be adopted.

The hon. gentleman has asked Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
the House to send the Bill to the Committee of the Whole, with instructions to do certain things. He cannot expect those of us who do not agree with some of his propositions to agree to the whole of them; and if he would consent to eliminate the 3rd and 5th clauses, and instruct the committee to adopt the others, there might not be any objection to his motion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: For the purposes of this motion I will agree to that.

I call the attention of the House to the fact that the only motion in order now is to refer the Bill back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines. We cannot now pass a motion giving instructions to the Committee of the Whole House. That would not be regular.

Of course, we could not give instructions to the Committee of the Whole House to do certain things which they are perfectly competent to do. I had to make this motion, which is the only one that is in order at this stage.
The regular procedure will be. if the hon. minister does not want the Bill referred to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, to withdraw the motion before the Chair.
I cannot withdraw my motion. I am right.
The motion is out of order. The order of the House is for the House to go into Committee of the Whole.
The motion in my hands is a motion to refer the Bill back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines. That motion is in order.

What was my great surprise at the opening of the present session to see what I considered an absolute breach of faith on the part of the trustees of the Atlantic and Lake Superior ? I learned that a Bill had been introduce In the Senate by which the Act of last session was entirely done away with. They - were relieved of the obligation of building three miles of the road, and they ask an extension of time for five years. As there was some doubt raised concerning the nature of the Bill introduced in the Senate and adopted by that body, I shall read it
1. The trustees of the bondholders of the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company, appointed by virtue of a deed of trust vesting* in them the property of the company, shall, notwithstanding any limitation of time contained in any Act, have all the powers for construction, completion and operation of the undertaking cf the company as were conferred originally on the company by the Acts relating to the company and by the Railway Act ; but the said powers shall not continue beyond the thirty-first day of December, one thousand nine hundred and seven, when they shall cease as regards any portion of the undertaking not then completed.
The county was placed in this position. It .wants this road to go ahead and the arrears "paid. The present company are not paying these arrears and do not wish to proceed with the extension of the road. I asked to have a clause inserted in that Bill providing that if the Gaspe and Western Railway should be incorporated, it should have no rights whatever in the county of Bona-venture until it acquired the Bale des Chaleurs Railway, eitiher by judicial sale or otherwise. That clause was inserted.
My second instructions were to have a provision inserted requiring the work to be commenced at Paspebiac within twelve months and that section extended to Port Daniel, the last parish in the county of Bonaventure, within those twelve months. That condition was inserted. My hon. friend from Gaspe (Mr. Lemienx) also had a clause put in the Bill providing that the work in Gaspe Basin must be completed in three years.
What possible objection can the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company have to the Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure).
Gaspe and Western Railway undertaking to pay those claims, if it chooses to do so. If the Gaspe and Western Railway undertake to pay these claims let it do so. My hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain), in opposing this Bill tooth and nail before the Railway Committee and defending the rights of the bondholders, completely overlooked the rights of the poor people, the rights of the labourers to be paid the claims due them in the county of Bonaventure. I would not have this Bill go through under any circumstances unless these claims due in Bonaventure are paid, and I may say that these claims are largely owing to Conservatives who were employed in the construction rf that railway by Mr. C. N. Armstrong. I am not standing up to-day for claims held by Liberals only in the county of Bonaventure, but claims held by .Conservatives as well. It is a matter of justice and fair play that these claims should be met, and these conditions having been inserted in this Bill under the instructions I have in my hand, my duty is to ask parliament to allow the Bill to go through. But the hon. member for Montmorency, after having been worsted in the Railway Committee, after having stood up in that committee solely for the rights of the bondholders, comes up now and asks us to insert a clause requiring this new company to deposit $100,000 before it can proceed with this undertaking.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if we were dealing with the Bank of Montreal or with the Canadian Pacific Railway or with the Grand Trunk Railway, or some other great concern of that nature, such a clause would be very reasonable. But is not the primary object of my hon. friend from Montmorency, having failed to have killed in the Railway Committee, to burden this new company with such conditions, that it wdl be unable to take over this work and construct the line ? We provide in this Bill that the road must be extended to Port Daniel within twelve months. The people of the eastern part of Bonaventure insist on having that portion of the road built. My hon. friend from Montmorency has a number of very warm friends in that portion of Bonaventure. There are parishes there in which a majority of votes were cast against me, but I am standing up here for the rights of those parishes, as I am standing up for those of the parishes that gave Liberal majorities. I ask the hon. member (Mr. Casgrain) to declare before this House whether he is looking first after the interests of the people of Bonaventure or is merely seeking to defeat this Bill in the interest of the bondholders. I do not object to the rights of the bondholders being secured. I want them to be protected. But they are. in .possesion of the road at the present moment, they have the first lien upon it, and the laws of the country protect them. But the unfortunate people who, for fifteen long years were exploited

by the railway ring which did such injury to the counties of Bonaventure and Gaspe have no protection, and it is to this parliament and to this government that they look for the protection of their interests. 1 hope, therefore, that hon. members on both sides, taking this into consideration, will see to it that nothing is inserted in this Bill which will in any way jeopardize the claims of'the unfortunate people who have been so badly treated for the last fifteen years.

1 shall not detain the House long, as I wish to say only a few words in explanation of the position I have taken on this question since its inception. Early in the session, I received from my electors in the county of Gaspe the same instructions that my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) received. I received a petition, and also resolutions which had been adopted by the county council and the different local councils asking me to oppose the two Bills which had been surreptitiously introduced in the Senate by the Atlantic and Lake Superior Railway Company. I had to oppose the two Bills, and I am glad to hear that the company has decided not to press for the adoption of these measures this year. Had the Bill been pressed by them, they would have been defeated in this House. As to the present Bill, the Gaspe and Western, X occupy the same position as does my hon. friend from Bonaventure. The county of Gaspd is the only county in the Dominion, with the exception of Charlevoix, deprived of railway communication. The Bill which is now before us, the Gaspe and Western, contained as at first presented, a clause which, if it had remained there, would perhaps have caused the defeat of the measure. Under that clause, the promoters would have been empowered to locate this railway in the interior of the peninsula of Gas-pfi. My instructions were to oppose the Bill on account of that clause. The people want the railway along the shore, and the promoters having agreed to build the railway along the shore, as near as possible the parishes situated along the Baie des Cha-leurs, and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, my electors are now perfectly satisfied. They have also joined with the electors of Bonaventure in asking the promoters that a clause be inserted by which the labourers in the county of Bonaventure should be paid. And I may say that many of these labourers are now residing in the county of GsapS. This amendment having been accepted by the promoters, together with other changes introduced by my hon. friend from Bonaventure and myself, the Bill is acceptable to both counties. I may say also that, in order to protect ourselves, we have asked the promoters to add to the board of provisional directors the names of Mr. Guite, ex-M.P., and Mr. A. T. Carter, warden of the county of Gaspe. With such a guarantee, this Bill is perfectly acceptable to my county, and I give it my fullest support and hope that the proposed amendments of my hon. friend from Montmorency will not be seriously discussed, because, if the promoters of this railway, besides the obligation imposed upon them by the amendments, were bound to deposit $100,000, they would be quite unable to go on with the work. I say that the obligations we have placed upon the company to pay the debts due by Mr. Armstrong and his associates, to build the section between Paspebiac and Gaspe Basin along the shore, to begin the work within one year and finish it within four, are as much as the company can undertake. To add a deposit of $100,000 can only be a means of defeating the object of the Bill.

The reason why I ask the House to give this Bill the six months' hoist is that the measure originated in a curious manner, as I am going to explain to the House. In 1897 a company was formed to build a railway from the Atlantic to Lake Superior, and that was the name of the company. The directors of this company were : Hon. ,T. .T. Thi-baudeau, Hon. Wm. Then the government asked the company to add three directors to be named by the government, which directors were : Wm. Baker, Cape Town, on the Baie des Chaleurs, Charles Chaput, Montreal, and Hon. J. W. Larue, Quebec. It was stipulated in this contract that the government would hold the company liable for the interest on the $8,000,000 arising from the bonds of the company, the government assuming the responsibility for the payment of this interest for a period of 20 years. The road was to be built from one end to the other according to the charter. Unfortunately, not long afterwards the Flynn government was defeated, and replaced by the government of the Hon. Mr. Marchand. Mr. Merchant! took with him as two of his colleagues, Mr. Duffy, as Minister of Railways and Public Works, and Mr. Arcliambault, as Attorney General. So when the company wanted to compel the government to fulfil the contract the latter pretended that the contract was illegal. They waited some time, and at last, forced more by their own friends than by

the company, the government decided to refer the question to the Court of Appeals. During that session I had the honour to represent my county in the legislature of Quebec. As I say, the government at that time referred this question to the Court of Appeals to decide. Mr. Flynn, the 'Chief of the opposition, was named by the company to defend their case, while Mr. Archambault and Mr. Duffy represented the government. Now, Mr. Speaker, when you compose a cabinet you generally take the most able and educated men for Minister of Railways and Attorney General-something like what we see in this Dominion government. The premier of the Dominion government always chooses a wise man to bo Minister of .Tus-tice. Well, these two able and educated men, Mr. Flynn and Mr. Archambault, pleaded the case of the government as well as they could, but their case was so weak that the Court of Appeals unanimously compelled them to fulfil their engagement towards the company. I say unanimously, but not quite, because on one point, though not an important point, there was one dissident. Mr. Justice Ouimet did not agree with the five or six other judges on one point ; and the Hon. Mr. Duffy told me personally that - Judge Ouimet had more brains than all the other judges together. Well, I think he is wrong. Anyway, when we saw the necessity of going on with the enterprise we presented a petition of right to get the consent of the government to sue them and compel them to fulfil their engagement. But we never succeeded in getting that permission from the government. During that time the company was so confident that they would get justice from the government that they undertook to build 20 miles of the Baie des Chajeurs Railway.	[DOT]

Ce que je veux dire, c'est que ce bill a origine dans l'iniquite; I wish I could say it in English, but I cannot. Well, I may say that no labourer and no creditor got anything. He could not be in the same place with Armstrong, because Armstrong was such a rascal. They thought they would succeed better by calling it the Gaspe short line running over the hills. Numerous petitions from the electors of Gaspe and Perce
district came here asking that the railway should pass along the shore, and so this year they changed their minds and decided to run the lines along the shore, and so this year they changed their minds and decided to run the lines along the rivers so as to make the people believe that they were going to build the road and that the company was very rich and going to buy out a syndicate and pay all the merchants and the labourers. They fee] very bad about the poor people and they are crying all the time that they are out of their money. I do not know whether I have permission to say it or not, but I want to state that they seem to be very much afraid of Armstrong. I will make a parallel with him and another gentleman who is here in this House, the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Raymond Prefontaine), and when there are some Bills to be passed this gentleman goes around and says : * Don't you pass that Bill, because Armstrong is in it : or, help me with this Bill because Armstrong is opposing it.' It was said that Armstrong had something to do with these Bills, and so they were sent to the Cimetiere des Innocents. Well, I think this present Bill should also be killed, but should not be placed with the innocents, as it is too guilty. I do not say that all the Liberals, but generally speaking the Liberal party is against Armstrong. If Armstrong passes on one side of the street they pass on the other, and if Armstrong is in town they say : 'There is some bad scheme going on because Armstrong is at the Russell.' Would you know the reason why they are so down on him ? I will tell you*: It is'because Mr. C. N. Armstrong once had a contract for the building of the Baie des Cha-leurs Railway and he had some subsidies coming to him from the Quebec government. He obtained $100,000 from the government. $100,000 was a big cheque, but what did he do ? Did he put it in his pocket and give nobody else anything ? No, he did not. What did he do with it ? House went into committee on Bill (No. 140) An Act to incorporate the Bishop of the Orthodox Russo-Greek Catholic Church for North America and Aleutian Islands, and each of the parishes and missions of the said church in Manitoba and the North-west Territories.-Mr. Oliver.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. When this Bill came before the House on different occasions 1 raised some objections on several grounds. First of all, we are asked to incorporate in Manitoba and the North-west Territories a church body whose members have never petitioned this parliament for incorporation. I can readily understand that such a community may need incorporation in order to organize and maintain their respective parishes in connection with their church work, but at the same time I think that the roundabout way in which this Bill has been introduced in this House is not at all regular. We had a petition presented to this House by the Right Rev. Mr. Tikhon, of San Francisco, California, claiming to be a bishop of the Orthodox Russo-Greek Catholic Church for North America and the Aleutian Islands, asking to be incorporated Mr. SPEAKER.
as a corporator sole, that is to say, as a corporation having the absolute privilege of controlling, not only the spiritual church matters, but the temporal matters as well in connection with this church. By the Bill subsequently introduced, the .prayer of that petition is fully granted, and the most reverend gentleman-as he is called in the Bill -is incorporated a corporation sole, with powers as defined in the Bill :
2. The corporation sola may receive and hold property of any kind for the uses and purposes of the Orthodox Russo-Greek Catholic Church in Manitoba and the North-west Territories, including the uses and purposes1 of any parish and mission, institution, college, school or hospital now or hereafter connected with the Orthodox Russo-Greek Catholic Church, and it may receive any devise by will, gift, deed, conveyance of land or any estate or interest therein," and sell, aJlienate, mortgage or lease any land's, tenements and hereditaments held by it.
Now, we have on different occasions, and even during the present session, incorporated bishops with similar powers. We incorporated, for instance, the bishop of Moosonee, by a Bill passed last week, but we knew that he was a bishop of the Church of England, we knew his status, as set forth in the recital of the Bill for his incorporation, and we knew he was a British subject, a resident in one of the dioceses, that bis diocese was a missionary one entirely, in the northern part of the territory of Keewatin, and that be could not have around him a personnel or a council capable of administering the affairs of bis church. We therefore very properly granted the prayer of his petition. But in this case we are granting the privilege of a corporation sole to a gentleman who is living in the city of San Francisco, who has no connection whatever with the people of the Northwest except that lie happens to be the chief official of the Greek Church, appointed 'by the Czar of Russia over that church. I said on a former occasion that I had no objection at all to providing machinery whereby the members of that church could go on with their own church work, and organize their missions and parishes, so long as the people themselves would have the administration of those missions and those parishes in their own hands and themselves asked for such privileges. But though the Bill was discussed in the Standing Orders Committee at great length and in the Private Bills Committee, we have never had any petition or information whatever with regard to the wish of the people most interested in this measure. No one came to represent those people and their views, and let us know their wishes and their wants. But in spite of all that, we have the Bill which is now before this committee and one which is not at all the Bill which was first introduced, owing to the multitude and variety of the amendments made to it in the Private Bills Committee.
In fact. Sir. I am surprised that such an important Bill should have been so amended

without it being reprinted and put in the hands of members of the House, so that they might be in a position to study the case. This Bill provides that this Rt. Rev. Bishop of San Francisco, shall be, as I have said, a corporation sole. But when I drew the attention of the Committee on Private Bills to the danger of granting such extensive powers to the gentleman who was a non-resident and who lived so far away from the parties interested in this measure, an amendment was introduced providing that any act, deed or conveyance affecting the properties of the church or any of the parishes in connection with the church- that is affecting their temporal affairs- should be countersigned by no less a gentleman than the Consul General of Russia, who lives in the city of Montreal. And, later on, a clause was added to the Bill providing that the corporation sole shall have and maintain a head office in the town of Edmonton, in the district of Alberta, in the North-west Territories.

For what purpose is the office ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. In order to receive service of any process of court that may require to be served on the church in general. So, Sir, you will see that, for the sake of establishing parishes and missions in the North-west, and having such an organization as this, it is proposed by the Bill to incorporate a bishop living in San Francisco and having a Canadian office in* the town of Edmonton, with the obligation upon him of getting ail the instruments in connection with temporal affairs countersigned by the Consul General of Russia, in Montreal. It is the most absurd piece of legislation ever introduced in this parliament. And, as 1 said before, it is introduced without the knowledge of the people directly interested in this legislation-they do not know the first thing about it. We are going to impose a very extensive, I may say absurd, piece of machinery upon them for tile control of the temporal affairs in connection of their church, and without their having asked for it. I am sure that if bon. members would consider this matter in an unbiased and impartial way, they would see that I was right in opposing the introduction of such legislation without first consulting the parties who were directly interested.
Now, what is the position of this clerical gentleman to whom we are giving control of matters in connection with the Greek Church ? The Galicians belonging to that faith who live in Manitoba and the Northwest are people from Austria. So far as nationality goes they were Austrians in their own country. And, now, we are to put them under the control of a bishop living in San Francisco, who has been appointed by the Czar of Russia Bishop of North America and the Aleutian Islands for the State Church of Russia. And, on the other hand,
we are exacting the signature of the Russian Consul General in Montreal to legalize any instrument that may be executed by' this bishop-a Consul General who has nothing in common with these people, as they do not belong to his nationality, except merely that they happen to profess the same religion as lie does. This, if it were carried out, would be a very bad piece of legislation, to my thinking. I have no objection to recognize the Russian-Greek Church or any other Greek Church, and to give people belonging to that faith the privilege of having their churches, their parishes and their missions. But what I object to is the machinery whereby these temporal affairs of the church will be administered. We do not know what troubles may follow. Orders may come from St. Petersburgh to these people, on some conscientious pretext to do this or do that, or refrain from doing this or that. We already have enough trouble with the Doukhobors, who. under conscientious pretext, are not willing to abide by the local laws of our country. They do not want to register their lands, they do not want to register their marriages, they do not want to do many things that are obligatory upon good citizens in this country. Who is to tell us that, later on, orders will not come from the church officials of the Greek Church in St. Petersburgh to their adherents, imposing duties upon them which will compel them to choose between their church membership and their citizenship ? But, apart from that altogether, I say that we ought to be very careful. There is more importance in this measure than appears. We are told: This is only a private Bill and we can amend it next year. Well, Sir, if there is such a feeling that we may require to amend it next year, I believe it will be far better to put the Bill off until next year, and then prepare and pass a measure that will be satisfactory to the people concerned and satisfactory to the country to which they have come to live. Perhaps I may be taxed with partiality in dealing with this matter. Sir, I have on every occasion endorsed and approved measures concerning other faiths than my own; because I, for one, recognize the fact that we live in a free country, that we ought to be liberal to others, even if we cannot think as they do. But, in this case, it is not a question of faith-it is a question of business, a question of property, yes, even a question of justice. I say that this parliament has no right to impose on a class of the community legislation for which they have not asked, and which we have no proof that they will accept.
Now, there is something very peculiar in the action of this right reverend gentleman in regard to this matter. In the petition that was presented before this pai'liament, and in the Bill as passed by the Private Bills Committee, he represents himself as the bishop of the Orthodox Russo-Creek Catholic Church for North America and the Aleutian

Islands. Since this Bill passed the committee, a hook has come into my hand? called the catechism of the Orthodox church; and in opening this little catechism-which I do not intend to read to this House-I find that this official book of the church is distributed with the blessing of the most Reverend Tikhon-tiie very same reverend gentleman who is asking for an Act of incorporation in this Bill-the most Reverend Tikhon, Bishop of the Orthodox Greek-Russian Church of North America. Now, Sir, if I go to the States, I find that in California the name of the church there is the Greek-Russian Slavonian Orthodox Eastern Church and Benevolent Society. That is the church over which this right reverend gentleman is presiding. If I go to Seattle, in the state of Washington, I find there that the church Is known as the Greco-Russian Orthodox Church of St. Spiridomus. Well, when we come to Manitoba and the North-west Territories we find there are two classes of Galicians, the one calling themselves Or-thodox-Greeks, and the other commonly styling themselves Greek Catholics. The Greek Catholics are a branch of the Roman Catholic Church, they call themselves Greek Catholics because their rite is the Greek rite; they do not follow the Latin rite. The others styling themselves Orthodox Greek, belong to the Greek rite also, but in connection with the Church of Russia.

One part of them inclines to the church of Russia, and to what church does the other half incline ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. The church of Rome.

Let them call themselves what they like, that makes no difference to us.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. What I object to is that this reverend gentleman introduces the word ' Catholic ' into this Bill, and asks us to acknowledge him under a designation that he does not use in any other country.

Nobody has a monopoly of that name.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Well you have not, I am sure of that.

That is all right. Will my hon. friend allow me to ask him a question, all jokes aside ? Do not the Episcopalians call themselves Catholics ? Answer that, yes or no.
ill1. LaRIVIERE. Well, the Episcopolians call themselves Catholics, but they do not ask me to admit that they are Catholics. I call myself a Catholic, but 1 do not compel any one else to call me a Catholic. At the same time, while Episcopolians call themselves Catholics-and I believe that they are using that privilege-they never asked this parliament to confirm them in their right thus to call themselves. They are liberal, they allow others to call themselves what-
Mr. LaRIVIERE.
ever they choose ; and we, with the same liberality, allow them to call themselves whatever they choose.

Supposing the Episcopalians did ask parliament to give them that name, would you object to it ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. Well, yes.

Why ?
Mr. LaRIVIERE. I do not object to them calling themselves whatever they choose, I grant them the privilege of calling themselves Catholic if they believe that they are so. Mr. Chairman, I see that I am treading on very delicate ground, and I regret it, because I wanted to object to this Bill at first on its general merits ; I did not want to go into these questions of theology or orthodoxy, on the contrary I wished to avoid them, and heretofore I have never mentioned them. But here this right reverend gentleman is known under a different name in San Francisco, and he goes to the North-west, where there is a mixed community, and asks us to acknowledge him a a Catholic. Well, as a Catholic I object to that.

The argument used by the hon. gentleman who has just addressed the committee (Mr. Lariviere) might be turned against himself and applied with equal propriety against the church which he represents. He objects that this church is controlled by a foreign power. So is the church of the hon. gentleman controlled by a foreign power, but does he object to that. We had something to say on that subject in connection with the Jesuits Estates Bill. But the arguments used by the hon. gentleman apply with equal propriety, with equal force in every instance, to the church to which the hon. gentleman belongs himself. With reference to the statement that the notice was not given, I think the usual notice was given ; everybody had notice that desired to have notice. With reference to the question whether any other church should call themselves Roman or Roman Catholic, except the one church, I think there is more than one church calling themselves Catholic.
Only one.

I admit that hon. gentlemen may think that they alone have a right to the name, but that does not prevent others

from using the name, as they certainly do. In my judgment therefore that is no serious objection to the Bill, and I do not think the argument which the hon. gentleman addressed to the House has any great force in it.

I do not propose to go into a discussion of this question on its merits. But the question was asked from my hon. friend from Provencher (Mr. LaRivi&re) what objections there were to the use of the word Catholic in the title of this Act of incorporation. Well, I do not know that there is any serious objection, there does not appear to be in the House at any rate, and no Catholic ought to object to that word in any Act of incorporation when he sees the great popularity of that name to-day. It appears to me there is a good parallel between this case and a Bill I accidentally heard discussed in the legislature of my own province some three years ago. We have in the province of New Brunswick and in the maritime provinces, and all over Canada, a very prominent body of Christians called Baptists. They were known as the Baptist Church. Some years ago they divided and formed two churches, Baptists still, but two distinct bodies. One portion, dissenting from the older body, took the name of the Free Christian Baptist Church and sought and obtained an Act of incorporation under that title. That new body divided again. A clergyman by the name of Osser, 1 think, differed in opinion from the majority, or, perhaps, as he claimed the minority of that body-I am not discussing that point-and he and his followers applied to the legislature of New Brunswick for an Act of incorporation. In asking for that Act of incorporation they wished to be designated by the name of the Free Baptist Church. While there was not much in the matter as they were Baptists too and no one could object that they should call themselves Baptists, when they came to the legislature for an Act of incorporation it was not the Catholic members that interfered but it was the Protestant members of the House. There was a very small number of Catholic members in the House and the whole debate was taken up by the Protestant members. They took the ground that while they were quite willing to give them an Act of incorporation, the use of the words ' Free Baptist ' in the Bill would create confusion, 'and it was something that they had no right to use because the word ' Free ' was in the Actj of incorporation of both other branches of that same church. While they gave them their Act of incorporation, they would not consent to the use of the word ' Free ' as proposed in the Bill. Therefore, I think my hon. friend can very well say that so far as the Galicians are concerned, being two distinct bodies so far as their religious belief is concerned, with this body applying for a charter to be incorporated into the Orthodox-Russo-Greek 147
Catholic church for North America and the Aleutian Islands. I do not see why this House should add anything to its title in giving the charter that is sought for now, I think it would be very simple to leave the word ' Catholic ' out.

The only objection which was taken to the Bill in the New Brunswick legislature was that this new church proposed to call itself the Free Baptist and in so doing was in reality calling itself by a name which was used by one of the other branches of the Baptist Church. This division of the church was called the Free Baptist and the fact that it was using the word ' free ' was objected to. It was the prefix that caused the trouble. In this case the name of the church is the Russo-Greek Catholic Church. There is no danger of any other body being confounded with that. I do not know whether our good friends the Episcopalians would call themselves the holy Catholic Church or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They do it in the church service.
It is the prefix that they used that caused the trouble.

speechtext:
The word ' free,' of course, was in the Bill which was before the House under consideration at that time, but the denomination that complained was not called the Free Baptist Church but it was called the Free Christian Baptist Church. They did not take the whole name, they used one word which was used in the title of the other church. In this case they are simply using a word here which does not belong to them.
Mr. LaRIVIERE. The right of a foreigner, an alien, to petition parliament is not recognized in the English system. My hon. friends will all remember the Cretan and the Boulogne cases. But in this country the practice has grown up of receiving petitions from aliens. As far as I can judge, that practice dates from 1878. On March lltli of that year, the attention of Mr. Speaker Anglin was called to a petition from some United States citizens interested in the Connecticut Mutual Insurance Company, praying for amendments to the Insurance Law, and after a very brief statement by Mr. Mackenzie, and without any discussion at all, Mr. Speaker Anglin decided that the petition would be received. It would appear from the brief debate, as reported in ' Hansard,' that those who spoke were under the impression that that was the English practice. I can state most emphatically that it is not. However, that practice, which was then initiated, has continued down to the present, and I suppose it would not lie in my mouth to claim that it should not be carried out in this instance.

The corporation sole shall have and maintain a head office at the town of Edmonton in the district of Alberta, and service of legal process at such head office shall be good and sufficient service of such process upon the corporation sole.
Well, the corporation sole may maintain a head office-that is an expression I never before heard of in connection with an ecclesiastical corporation-the ecclesiastical corporation is to have a head office in the town of Edmonton. However, passing by that curious word, suppose the ecclesiastical corporation does not happen to have a head office at Edmonton, where are you under this Bill ? The clause has not been drafted with sufficient care. It should go further and provide that in the event of the corporation sole not opening a head office in the town of Edmonton, service upon the corporation could be effected by service of process upon a priest or some person connected with the corporation in that particular district ; otherwise this clause 8 is of no service whatever. Or service might be effected by letter addressed to it, or by publication. The clause in its present shape is absolutely ineffectual, it seems to me ; and I would suggest it should be amended by stating that the domicile of the corporation shall be at such and such a place in this country, and that the head office-call it that-should be opened in that particular place, and that in default of such head office being opened, service on the corporation can be effected by service upon some priest, or by posting up the service in the town hall, or something of that kind.
Or that it shall have a registered address.
But it may not have a registered address.
It may be required to have.

If you do require it, it may not observe that provision. You must have a provision that the service of the process may be made by posting it up, or by advertising it in the newspapers, or something of that kind.
That is a matter of procedure.
But it must be dealt with by this Bill.
I do not think it is necessary, because if the head office is stated to be at Edmonton, it will be for the provincial court to determine the manner of making a service.

If the hon. gentleman's argument is sound that the provincial courts can deal with the matter, it is perfectly clear that this parliament should have nothing to do with it. I do not know whether there is any procedure in the province of Manitoba or in the North-west Territories to cover a ease of this kind. So far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned I can say that there is no procedure that I am aware of to cover a case of this kind, and I suppose we are not to pass this Bill with an understanding that this provision is ineffectual unless we know something about the procedure of Manitoba and the North-west Territories. I do not think we should leave it to provincial enactment. We are doing a somewhat extraordinary thing when we incorporate a person who not only lives but proposes to live outside of the jurisdiction. It may be all right, but let us provide that he shall have his domicile inside the jurisdiction, and also provide some effectual mode of service upon him within the jurisdiction.

As a member of the committee which suggested this amendment to the Bill I may say that perhaps the wording may yet be somewhat Improved. I think if the hon. member who has made this suggestion would agree to an amendment providing that a registered letter addressed to this corporation at the town or city where they happen to have their head office under this Bill would be a sufficient service the objections would be removed. Personally, I feel, that as long as this country recognizes the right to grant incorporation to these religious and semi-religious bodies, entitling them to hold property, I do not see why it should refuse to do so in this case. As there is a considerable number of these people in the North-west Territories, I thiuk they should have the same privileges as all other people in this country and that an Act of incorporation should be given to them so that their religious bodies may be entitled to hold property for their own purposes. I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that it should be made clear that the only power we give under this Bill is the right of these people to hold property, and that carries with it the right to sue and be sued. This ought to be perfectly clear as the hon. lender of the opposition has pointed out. If any person has a claim against this church it must be perfectly clear that nothing in the Bill shall allow them to evade
the laws of the country. The desire of the committee was that they should receive this Act of incorporation without doing an injustice to any other person, and that they should be held amenable to the laws of the country the same as any other person or corporation.

This Bill which I have in my hand entitled ' An Act for the relief of Samuel Nelson Chipman ' calls upon me as a member of the House to act in a judicial capacity. I was not present at the trial of this case; I heard none of the testi-moiiy; I do not know whether that testimony was properly presented and duly weighed or not. I do not suppose that there is a member of this House who is called upon to act in a co-ordinate capacity with the Senate in this matter who is in a position to exercise judicial functions in this case properly. Of course I shall not move that tbisl Bill shall not pass, but I protest as I have often protested against the method of granting divorces in this country. I say that we are not in a position to act judicially in this matter and that it is a scandalous thing-I use the word advisedly -it is a scandalous thing that this practice is adhered to in this Dominion of Canada. If a divorce is to be granted at all, of course the law must define what is the cause and what is the offence that will warrant the granting of that decree. If a divorce is granted because the provisions and requirements of the law have been transgressed, it is a question of evidence as to whether the party applying for the divorce is entitled to that divorce. I repeat that I know nothing about this evidence; I am in no position to act on this evidence as a judge ought act. The evidence comes to me in a sense in a hearsay way; I have not heard the evidence; I have not seen these parties arraigned ; I have not heard these parties questioned; I do not know what the method of carrying on this trial was, and I again repeat that if a divorce under any circumstances is proper to be granted; it should be granted by a legal tribunal. The whole system we have been pursuing in the Dominion since confederation is on a false basis, and I shall avail of the privilege, if I am spared another session, to bring a resolution before this House affirming the principle that the method of granting divorces in Canada is not a well-founded and proper method, and that if divorces are to be granted at all the law should define clearly what is the offence that will warrant the granting of the divorce, and that the

case shall be referred to a proper legal tribunal. .

I may say that I am quite willing to move that these amendments be agreed to, but, in consequence of these amendments, I think some verbal alterations will have to be made in section 10. The first amendment is to section 2 of the Bill, which was passed by this House. In addition to the words ' No. 1 ' the senators want to put in ' or XXX ' which I think is quite right. That comes in the fourth line of section 6 of the original Act. Then, the senators, move in amendment to section 10 to strike out the word ' inspectors.' Section 10 of the Act says:
Every person who wilfully alters, effaces or obliterates wholly or partially, or causes to be altered, effaced or obliterated, any inspector's marks on any package which has undergone inspection, shall incur a penalty of forty dollars.
1 have no objection at all to that, but I wish to insert, after ' who ' in the first line of section 10, the words * not being an inspector,' so as to provide that an inspector may efface certain marks when he finds that they have been wrongfully placed upon a package. Otherwise this amendment would interfere witli section 9 of the same Act. I therefore move :
That these amendments be concurred in, but that in section 10 of the said Act, in'the'first line, after the word ' who,' the words ' not being an inspector ' be inserted.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I would like to direct the attention of the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and of the lion. Minister of Labour (Mr. Mulock) to the dispatches which appeared in the morning papers as to the continuation of the strike amongst the employees of the loco-

motive works at Kingston. I notice a dispatch in the Montreal ' Gazette ' to-day dealing with the matter, and it is as follows :
Ottawa, May 11-(Special).-A report which comes from Kingston is to the effect that aliens are being imported into that town to take the place of striking machinists in the locomotive works. It is said that these aliens are employed on the locomotives which are being constructed there for the Intercolonial Railway. The attention of the government will probably be called to the report to-morrow.
In this morning's ' Citizen ' there is a more lengthy despatch, as follows :
Kingston, May 11-(Special).-No settlement has yet been arrived at between the striking machinists and the Kingston locomotive works. The company, contrary to the provisions of the alien labour law, is importing foreigners to take the place of the strikers to do work on government contract locomotives. Ralph Smith, M.P., president of the Dominion Trades and Labour Congress, was agreed upon as arbitrator of the conflicting interests, but the company refused to be bound by his decision; therefore, Mr. Smith refused to act further.
Mr. Robert Glockling, of the Ontario Labour Bureau, has been here at the instance of Hon. Frank Latchford, Minister of Public Works, to endeavour to bring about a settlement, but has been unsuccessful. Mr. Glockling, it is said, has reported to his minister that the company is entirely to blame, and if a speedy settlement is not made, the chances of the Liberal candidate. Mr. E. J. B. Pease, for re-election, are decidedly slim.

Holmes, organizer of the International machinists' union, is still here looking after the interests of the strikers.
It is understood that the Minister of Labour, Hon. Wm. Mulock, will step into the breach at the solicitation of the machinists and depute Mr. Mackenzie King, Deputy Minister of Labour, to visit the city to enforce the alien labour law, and also strive to effect an immediate settlement of the differences.
I would like to ask the right hou. leader of the government or the lion. Minister of Labour what special effort has been made to prevent the importation of aliens into Kingston to do work in connection with these locomotives, and if their attention has been drawn to the fact that aliens are coming in, and also to know if the hou. Minister of Labour has moved' in the direction of sending his deputy up to try and bring about a settlement of the dispute which so unhappily exists between the machinists and their employers. It seems to me, that, in view of the fact that the government gave a contract for twenty locomotives, without tender, to the locomotive works at Kingston, they are specially called upon to see that in carrying out a contract of this kind, union wages are paid to the men engaged in the work. If the statements made in both of these papers are true, I submit respectfully that it is a duty incumbent upon the government to see to it that the men who are out on strike for a fair wage shall not be
handicapped by aliens being permitted to take their places in contravention of the Alien Labour Act. I would like to have a statement from the First Minister, or from the Minister of Labour, as to what has been done already and as to what the government intend to do in the future in reference to the matter.

The government has received no information from any source that there is any infraction of the Alien Labour Act, at Kingston or that such infraction is intended. Neither the government nor any member of it, nor the Department of Labour, has beeen asked to intevene by either party for the settlement of the dispute, and until invited it would not be likely to produce any good results should the department intervene.
