The hon. gentleman (Mr. Brock) denies this. But 1 can assure him that 1 'have seen it with my own eyes. And I had the assurance of those who had placed the notices in their shop windows that that was the reason for appealing to the people-that the people had a kindly feeling towards Canada because of the preference. But supposing that we had obtained that preference which lion, gentlemen opposite think we ought to have obtained-supposing that owing to the representations of the Canadian government and people, Great Britain had imposed a tax upon the food of her working people-is it conceivable that tTinse working people would have been favourably disposed towards those who had been tiie means of imposing that tax upon them V Is it conceivable that the breadwinners in the cities of Great Britain would have been disposed to buy the articles sent to them by the people who were the cause of increasing the price of their loaf ? I do not think it is conceivable. 1 believe that, on the contrary, the working people of the large industrial centres in England would have cursed the name of Canada, and would have tried their best to injure Canadian trade in Great Britain, instead of supporting and encouraging it. The hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) a few moments ago, referred to a supposed change of public opinion in England in favour, of protection, and quoted the imposition of these taxes as evidence. The hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has given the first result of the imposition of bread taxes upon the English electors by showing that in the city of Bury, one of the very centres in which Canadian products are received with favour, the electors, who, a few years ago, elected a supporter of the present government by a large majority, had rejected another supporter of that government by an almost equally large majority; and the battle was entirely fought ouit on the question of bread taxes, and the change amongst the electors was entirely due to the adoption of that policy by the government. Now, that is an expression of the feeling that exists amongst those people. Had we in Canada been responsible for the imposition of that bread tax, we should have antagonized the great industrial class of the mother country. 1 venture to say that not only would that be a great detriment to the trade in our food products, but it would have beeu one of the greatest hindrances to that movement for Imperial unity, one of the first steps in which was the preference that we granted to Great Britain. Had we adopted that plan, and had we obtained that result- which 1 do not for a moment think we could have obtained as a matter of fact- we would have brought about this condition of affairs-that the breadwinners of England would Have felt aggrieved against the colony and would have felt that the colonies had asked them to tax themselves for the benefit of colonial producers. Instead of having the people almost unanimously in favour of the colonies, w,e would 'have had them divided into two great camps, one opposed to everything colonial because of the sense of grievance against the colony, and the other the feeling that they were helped a little by the fact that the products of their farms had been increased in price by the imposition of these taxes. But to-day we are in an entirely different position. When" we adopted the preference we reduced the taxes upon our own people. That is a point that lion, gentlemen opposite do not consider. It is not part of their policy to think of reducing the burden upon the taxpayer. All they want to do is to pile on taxes for the purpose of protection. When we gave the preference, we relieved our people of a burden. When we wish to secure a preference in Great Britain, we wish also to'remove a part of the burden of taxation resting upon those people. The condition to-day is such that we can do that. My right hon. friend can go ** "d ask for the remission by Great Britain, so far as the colonies are concerned of the tax on breadstuffs in part or altogether. When we do that-we shall have the sympathy of the breadwinners of the old land, and they will feel that the colonies are acting in their favour. We shall have the support of these people, instead of their direct antagonism. It seems to me, therefore, that we are in a much better position to-day than we should have been had we tried in 1897 to make a bargain and had succeeded. We can make a bargain to-day, but we could not make one then without injuring a portion of our fellow subjects in the old laud. I do not wish Canada to occupy that position.
Now, Sir, I will say one word more in regard to the question in England. I am not going to say for one moment what should be tlxe policy of Great Britain. That is for them to decide, just as it is for the people of Canada to decide our policy. It would be unfortunate if we were to be hampered in the exercise of our independent right in deciding upon our own policy, and I wish to give the same freedom to the people of the old land, to the people of Australia, and to the people of all the other colonies. But I do believe that we cau do it off our own bat, if I may use the expression, in the interest of the rest of the empire, just as in 1897, we gave a preference to the people of Great Britain in our own markets without asking anything in return. Speaking for myself I venture to think that Sir Michael Hieks-Beaeh the other day when he introduced his corn duties, missed a great opportunity. If lie had then, without any consultation with the colonies, given them immediately a preference in that iinposi-

tion of the corn duties. I believe he would have done a great stroke of statesmansnip in the Interest of the empire, and in strengthening the bonds uniting the various portions of the empire. But if he did not desire tKn do that then, I believe he is still in a position to give a preference to colonial products which will help the situation, and do a great deal to strengthen the ties between the motherland and her colonies.
I want one thing to be noticed, that in all the discussions in the parliament of Great Britain, Sir Michael Hicks-Beach himself, Mr. Balfour, the leader of the House, and all the other speakers in support of the government, distinctly declared that this imposition of a bread tax, is in no sense a reversion to protection. So emphatically have they declared this that as a matter of fact in Great Britain to-day this tax is not looked upon as involving the issue between free trade and protection, although the Liberal party are rather disposed to bring it forward as a line of cleavage between the two parties on the issue of free trade and protection. But the accepted opinion in Great Britain is that this tax is not a protectionist tax but a revenue tax.

I do not wish them to think it was brought about by the colonies. I would be sorry to have them think that any preference had been given to Canada which would hurt the people of Great Britain to such an extent that they would feel aggrieved towards us. On the contrary, I wish, when any preference is given to Canada by Great Britain, that it shall come from the people of Great Britain just as freely as the preference which we gave to Great Britain, without any bargaining and without asking anything in return. That is the feeling I have always had in regard to this preference. I stated over and over again in Great Britain that Canada gave that preference freely without asking anything in return ; and I hope the time will come that Great Britain, now that she has put a food tax upon her people, will give a preference to the colonies and relieve her own people without imposing a duty upon them. I believe that such a preference would do more Hon. Mr. FISHER.
than any act looking towards military defence or affecting political relations, to strengthen the ties that bind the different parts of the empire together, and make the empire stronger to face the world when it becomes necessary for her to face me world.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) feels himself in an awkward situation in view of what England has done lately. He said : When he was over there we did not want any preference, that what we had done we had done freely, generously and liberally. He said also that although we had made no demands for a preference we have practically a preference in the markets of the mother country. He did not offer any proof of his statement, nor did he show that our preference to the mother country had resulted in any advantage to us in the English market over what we have in the market of the United States or of other countries. If he looks up the trade returns since this preference was given, he will find that the whole argument is against his contention, for they show that we have not benefited in any material respect on account of that preference. He says the working people of England would look witli disfavour upon Canada if a tax was put upon their bread for the benefit of Canada. But it has been put on. If the hon. gentleman desires to get into the good graces of the working people of England the first thing he should do would be to try to relieve them of that tax by letting our wheat in free, by letting the grain of the colonies in free, and by that means supplying the nation with their breadstuff's. The colonies could readily supply all the breadstuffs of the English people in a short time. So if his argument is worth anything it can be turned against himself. The policy of the present government, he says, has not been to pile on the taxes. Who takes $10,000,000 of taxes more out of the people than their predecessors ? Is it not the present government ? Who raises a larger revenue if it is not the present government ? Who makes a larger expenditure if it is not the present government ? So I say that instead of not piling on more taxes the whole history of this administration is an argument to the contrary.
The hon. gentleman for North Norfolk (Mi'. Charlton) said that the result of an election in England adverse to the government was due to the bread tax imposed. He said that shows the sentiment of the British people. Then I say if he desires to have the sentiment of the British people in his favour let us tell the English labouring men that we desire to take off that bread tax and supply them with their bread free. That is one of the strongest arguments that could be addressed to the British people. The hon. member for North Norfolk goes on to say that we should not do this for fear of offend-

ing our friends to the south. I have heard that argument addressed to this House for 24 years in succession, and it seems to me the most humiliating, the most debasing argument that could ever be addressed to a free people. Are we not here an independent and integral part of the British Empire with rights of our own, with duties of our own to perform 1 Have we not to look after the interest of our own people, and can we not do it without fear of offending any other nation in the world ? Why, we would be little better than slaves if we cringed before any other nation. We ought to be ashamed of ourselves as British freemen to say that because of the fear of offending the nation to the south of us we are afraid of doing what it is our duty to do as members of the Canadian parliament.
That lion, gentleman has always addressed that argument to the House and I think it is unworthy of him and unworthy of any British subject in the Dominion of Canada. Our great danger, he says, is a struggle that [DOT]some day may come with our American [DOT]friends to the south that may take every man and every dollar that we have and that then the result will be doubtful, and he gives that'as his reason why we should not do anything along the line of Imperial defence or even consider Imperial defence with the mother country. He is afraid that we may offend our neighbours to the south of us. Would that not be the strongest reason that we should prefer to do our part in the defence of the British Empire so that neither the United States nor any other country in the world would dare attack us either on the high seas or on the lakes ? Should it be a matter of offence to the American people ? Even if it should be a matter of offence we should be unworthy of ourselves if we regarded it as a reason why we should not join with the mother country in considering the question of Imperial defence. The hon. gentleman says that we should not be bound by hard and fast rules in regard to national defence. My answer is that it is not necessary. The hon. gentleman went on to say that we have done a great deal for national defence. Why did we build the Canadian Pacific Railway that will be available for the transport of troops from the east to the west and from the west to the east, and for bringing the forces from one pai*t of the empire to another ? Was it because of any hard and fast rules ? Not at all. I see no reason why we should be bound down by hard and fast rules, but we should work upon intelligent lines jointly with the mother country, and we should have an intelligent understanding as to what are the best lines to be adopted. We should not be bound down by hard and fast rules, but there is a strong reason why we should talk it over and come to an understanding as to what is best to be done on the part of the colonies and the mother country, so that we shall act upon intelligent lines and be able to benefit by the understanding arrived at in
time of need. Then the right hon. the leader of the government says : Formulate a resolution for us and we will see whether we can accept it; or in other words, make a policy for us. and if it is acceptable we will adopt it. The hon. gentlemen have been stealing our clothes too long and they are reform misfits up to the present. They want to do a little more of that same kind of thing. If we were to move a resolution he would call upon his supporters to vote it down, because it would be a motion of want of confidence. We have introduced this subject in the way in which it has been introduced so as to avoid that possibility and in order to secure the freest possible discussion ; yet, the right hon. gentleman says: Formulate a policy. We are asking the right hon. gentleman to say whether lie is prepared to discuss commercial and political relations along the lines that we have indicated. It is for the purpose of enabling the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues to understand what the sentiments of this House are that we have made the proposition we have to-night and we have done it in such a way as not to embarrass him, but for the purpose of having the freest discussion so that he may understand that he carries with him the sentiments of the Canadian parliament. He does not require us to formulate a policy for him, because if these hon. gentlemen are not fit to formulate a policy for themselves they should not be there. The Canadian people should put others in their places who are able to formulate a policy that will be suited to Canadian needs and interests. The Prime Minister says that they are going over there and for what purpose ?-To listen. He reminds me very much of a bashful maiden who wants to be wooed but will not make any proposals. He is the Prime Minister of the Dominion of Canada, one of the most important parts of the British empire. He goes to the conference and the representatives of the empire there say : Bet us have a free conference to see what we had better do. He says : I am not going to take part in the discussion but I am going to listen. He is like a shy maiden sitting in the corner, waiting to be coaxed out and to be asked, will you do this or not. He says : We will listen and if they propose something that meets our views we will accept it and if they do not we will come home practically with our fingers in our mouths. That is the sum and substance of what he is going to say and do there. Yet. as the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) says, here is a golden opportunity. Parliament is in session and he can get the views and the assistance of parliament to strengthen his hands in the negotiation, but he does not desire to have them. Now, we have not thought it necessary during this session to introduce a resolution. Why ? For the purpose of giving the right hon. gentleman an opportunity of asking parliament for its opinion in reference to these

questions. We expected that he would take advantage of the opportunity before parliament prorogued to ask an expression of opinion from the Canadian parliament as to what lie should do at the conference, upon what grounds lie should consider this question and ns to what he should be free to propose to the British people. But. the right hon. gentleman does not want anything from England. If Great Britain proposes preferential trade, he says, we will be prepared to consider whether we shall accept it. The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) says -that it is not our place to ask it, but if Britain proposes it we will accept it. How under heaven is Great Britain likely to propose it if every member of the government who goes home tells the people there that we do not want it and that we do not look for it ? They say that such a policy is unsuitable for us and unsuitable for them and they say if England offers it we will consider it. Is England likely to offer it when the people there have been told that we do not want it ? Hon. gentlemen have already given England the strongest excuse for not proposing it. The right hon. gentleman says that wlmt was not possible in 1807 may be possible now. But he has told them that we do not want it whether if Is possible or not. Then the right hon. gentleman does not propose to discuss the question. He has told us that he is going over there to sit and listen and not to propose. Is England likely to propose what she has been told Canada does not want ? No. her statesmen are too astute and her diplomats know that a hint is as good as plain statement. Therefore the right hon. gentleman is not likely to get preferential trade. The free trade preferential tariff was a wonderful measure of tariff reform and it was based on the reform misfit principle, it does not tit Canada. It is of no use to Canada and of very little value to England, but it has done great harm to some of the most important industries in Canada. The right hon. gentleman says that we do not want to discuss the question of our political relations, and lie tells us that they are ajl right. He says that we do not want to discuss the question of Imperial defence, that we do not want to touch that. As the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Hag-gart) stated the British Empire may be attacked in any part of her colonies and it is the decisive battle there fought that will tell whether Canada is to be free and whether it is still to be Canada. The battle which is then being fought will be the battle of Canada as well as Britain. Canada must be prepared to take her part in the conflict and to give her assistance in defence of the British empire no matter where the battle may lie fought. But. why should we uot confer with the British empire as to what may be done along intelligent lines so that each integral part of the empire can come to this conflict in support of file empire prepared to do its part in the defence of that empire ?
If the Prime Minister carries out his in-

tention not to discuss Imperial defence I can tell him that there is not an Anglo-Saxon in the British Empire who will not declare that he has done less than his duty. If he will not discuss the defences of the empire with the representatives of the other colonies he is-I was going to say, unworthy of the name of British and unworthy the position he occupies as Prime Minister of the first colony In the empire. We have been told over and over again in this House that our political relations cannot remain in the future as they have been In the past. The right hon, gentleman lias told us many a time that lie can foresee the day coming when we will have reached that ripe age that we shall become a nation ourselves. That Indicates that the right lion, gentleman believes that a change is going on in our political standing. The premier of the first British colony knowing that and telling the Canadian people that yet proclaims in the same breath that he will refuse to discuss our relationship with the empire with a view of continuing those ties which have bound us to the mother land in the past and strengthening them. But the right lion, gentleman says he will discuss our commercial relations. lie will sit in the corner and lie will say to the others :	Make your proposals and I will
consider them. He admits that we want to extend our trade and to open up new markets, but he says that he will have no proposals to make at the conference. He has not the genius of statesmanship to the extent of possessing enough initiative to enable him to make proposals as regards his own country to the representatives of the other colonies. He will not tell them what his own country requires, hut he will take chances on their knowing better than he does the needs of Canada, and when they tell him what Canada wants he will consider whether he will accept it or not. Why, Mr. Speaker, a man who is so reticent and bashful that at such a conference he cannot tell what his country wants is not the right man to represent Canada on such a mission. Our representative should be as free to make proposals in the interest of his country as would be tbe premier of any other colony, or the representatives of Great Britain. If the right hon. gentleman fails to place the needs of this country before that important body he will do less than the Canadian people expect of him. He is going over there to represent the executive of this government, but he does not want to represent the parliament of his country. That is evident from the fact that the right hon. gentleman declines to ask the advice of the Canadian parliament. Far from asking for such advice lie spurns it when tendered, and he refuses to be fortified by the strength which the Canadian parliament could lend to his efforts. Now is the time when he can obtain the opinion of parliament if he desires it. Parliament is ready to support him in

making demands which would be for the welfare of Canada and of the British Empire, but to-night he rejects the assistance of parliament. He goes to that conference silently to represent the executive, his whole action is very much like unto the deal which that executive made In connection with the Yukon railway, in which case they found out afterwards that they were not in harmony with the sentiment of the country, and perhaps not in harmony with themselves. He tells us that the country wants preferential trade to-day. He ought to know that for he has been told it in a thousand ways. The boards of trade, the municipal corporations, the commercial and agricultural interests of the country have pronounced to him in favour of preferential trade. He admits that the conditions have changed. Formerly he told us that he would not ask for preferential trade from Great Britain because England would not grant it ns she would not abandon her free trade principles and tax her breadstuffs. But England has changed her policy, and now that there is an opportunity to get preferential trade the premier does not desire to ask for it. Well, the right lion, gentleman is practically going It blind. He is going to represent Canada at an important imperial conference and he is going without ascertaining the views of the Canadian people through their representatives in parliament. If parliament had not been in session for some months past I could perhaps understand the attitude of the right lion, gentleman, but the fact that he refuses to take the advantage of-parliament which he can now readily obtain is absolutely inexplicable. He keeps the country and parliament in the dark and lie apparently desires to be in the dark himself. He is treating Canada and the parliament of Canada with scant courtesy, hd refrains from disclosing to parliament what he intends to do and in view of his entire conduct we are justified in bringing this matter to his attention. And if, when the right lion, gentleman returns home we find he has disregarded the advice tendered from this side of the House he cannot blame us if we call him severely to task for his sins of omission as well as his sins of commission in connection with this matter.

M- ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Mr. Speaker, I think it is very unfortunate that it is not the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) who is going to represent the interests of Canada in England instead of the premier. If he would not by argument convince the Imperial government as to their duty, he might succeed better by scolding them, as he generally does in this House. I have not spoken much on this subject when it has been under discussion, and I do not intend to occupy much of the time of the House to-night. Hon. gentlemen opposite appear to take great consolation from the idea that there is a disturbing element in the government. Well, I think we on this side of the House have the confidence of the government at least as much as hon. gentlemen opposite, and we have not heard a hint of anything but the greatest unanimity of sentiment among our friends in the government, and we at least have the happy gssurance that there is unanimity on the part of their supporters to keep them in the position they at present occupy. Hon. gentlemen opposite appear to take great consolation from the position of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte). It appears that he made an after-dinner speech somewhere. Now, I do not know that any member of the government should be held responsible for an after-dinner speech. The only after-dinner speeches we hear of for which governments are to be held responsible are those made at the Lord Mayor's dinner in London at which the government announce their general policy and the relationship of the empire with other countries. But that was not the case witli my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works. When you think of the horrible pit and the miry clay out of which he escaped when he left the party on the other side of the House and came over to this side, it is almost a miracle that he is as pure as he is. If there is any element of protection in his policy, it is because he has not been perfectly emancipated from the ideas that were once promulgated on that side of the House. To my hon. friend I would say, beware of the leaven of the Pharisees; do not take any advice from that side of the House, and if you will be guided by the advice of your friends, the supporters of the government, you will occupy a sure position and the country will sustain the government of which you are one of the brilliant members.
A good deal has been said about the condition of England and the curse that free trade has been to England. I think it was my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gourley) who dwelt upon Cobden and Bright as being the curse of England. But if you look at the condition of England since she adopted free trade, you will find that no country in the world has acquired such greatness or so extended her trade as Great Britain did under her free trade policy. The moment the present government adopt a protective policy, it will be sure to go down. I believe that to-day, if a general election took place in Great Britain, the present government would be defeated because of the small measure of protection they have adopted on wheat and bread.

What about the election that took place yesterday ?
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I am going to speak of that. I have in my

hand a paper which, referring to the cotton trade of Great Britain, says
A recent issue of the ' Commercial Intelligencer ' published statistics which show that Great Britain has more than double the number of cotton spindles in operation that the United States has, and that, apart from the latter country, Great Britain has more spindles than all the rest of the world put together.
Then it goes on to say that Great Britain has 45,500,000 spindles manufacturing cotton, while the United States, which produces the raw material, has only about 20,000,000. Here is the article of cotton, carried in British ships from Egypt and from the Southern States, manufactured in England and sent to all parts of the world to compete with the rest of the world ; although cotton is a material England does not produce. No other country in the world could have succeeded in doing this, nor could England except under her free trade policy.
We have dwelt perhaps too much on what we have achieved in South Africa. I, for one, do not consider, and have not considered from the very outset, that Canada has done as much as we ought to have done in defence of the empire in South Africa. When you compare what Canada has done with what has been done by New Zealand and Australia, I hesitate to say that we have done our duty in that respect.

The very same thing.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) We have not the number of men in South Africa today that those other colonies have; but there is one thing certain, that Great Britain need not be afraid, if assistance is wanted, but that Canada will be prepared to do her duty both on land and on sea. When sailors are wanted to supply the navy, we shall be prepared to give our fishermen of Nova Scotia, and they will not be a month on board the ships before they will be just as active as the men who were there before them.
The friends of the government will send to England the premier and the other members of the government with him to discuss the trade policy; and we have the utmost confidence that they will protect the interests of Canada as far as they can be protected; but I do not think that they will be in a position, even supported by the premiers of the Commonwealth of Australia and New Zealand, to dictate to the Imperial government what they shall do; and I have very serious doubts indeed that, with all the interests involved, you will find Great Britain agreeing to preferential trade in favour of the colonies as against the rest of the world. If they will, we will all rejoice. But I have great doubts that the empire will give a preference to Canadian products against the products of other countries. Every step this government takes should be a step, not towards Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.).
protection, but towards reducing the duties lower and lower, and the lower you make the tariff the higher revenue you will get.
This question is being discussed in the Australian pa.peirs. Cable intelligence has been received in the ' Herald ' of late to the effect that in Australia public attention is directed to the fact that Canada is desirous of bringing about closer trade relations with Australia. The Canadian government proposed meeting the representatives of Australia and New Zealand in London for the purpose of taking various intercolonial matters into consideration, and the premier of the Commonwealth recently cabled our Prime Minister his consent to that proposal. I have some hopes that perhaps an arrangement for preferential trade or free trade may be established by this means between Canada and the other colonies. That is a practical subject and one that may to some extent be accomplished; but I do not think that, with all the influence which the premiers of the different colonies will bring to bear on the government of England, they will spcceed in convincing that government to give a preference in favour of the colonies against the rest of the world.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been very free in giving advice to the government, but the government have been very cautious in accepting advice from their opponents. They would rather take advice from their friends. Well, their friends prefer that they should go home to London untrammelled by any advice, because we have full confidence in the Prime Minister and those associated with him. We believe that they will do everything possible in the interests of Canada, and prefer that they should go across untrammelled, and not limited even to the views that may be expressed by some of their own .supporters, because we know that they will do everything possible in the interests of this Dominion. The eyes of the whole Dominion will be on them, and the whole Dominion is satisfied that they will do all that can reasonably be expected and all that any men in their position could do. Should they fail in any particular, it will not be because they have not advocated the interests of Canada to the most of their ability. I had taken quite a number of notes, but at this hour I shall not delay the House longer, and I shall conclude by repeating that the right lion, the First Minister and the other members of the government, if they should require any advice, should rather seek it from their friends than accept it from their opponents.

The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Ross) tells us that when the right bon. the First Minister and his colleagues go to Great Britain, the eyes of Canada will be upon them. In that opinion I quite agree. Not only wiill that he the case then, but the eye's of Canada are upon the government to-night, and have been since the beginning

of this session, and their ears have been open to ascertain whether the government were going to take the country into their . confidence or not. This is a momentous time in the history of Canada. It is a momentous time in the history of the empire. Two terms are, to a great extent, concurrent and synoinous, because the prosperity of Canada is inevitably wrapped up in the destiny of Britain. In these months that have gone by, I think I am right in saying that the people of Canada dad expect, and had a right to expect, that at such a momentous time, when such great issues are involved, both to Canada and the empire, the government would have regarded it as their duty not to wait for the opposition, not to wait for anybody, but of their own initiative to bring before this House a resolution for discussion covering the various matters which must come up for discussion at the colonial conference to be held during the Coronation ceremonies-in Britain I would rather be wrong than diliy dally and 1 want to lay down as my view, whether right or wrong, that it is of the essence of constitutional government that when a great question of this kind arises, the administration should take the representatives of the people into their confidence and discuss in parliament the questions that arc to be submitted at that conference. Instead of that, tiie government, although invited from time to time-and I was one of those who suggested it to the government during this session-the government although frequently urged to lay some broad proposition before parliament for public discussion and ventilation, have seen fit to adopt the policy of silence. And I charge, on behalf of the people of Canada, that the government lias been recreant tolls duty with regard to this great question. We have to-night a discussion which transcends, I believe, in humiliating the administration before tiie people of Canada, even those discussions we have had previously in this session-and this session has not been unmarked by humiliating positions for the government of this country. What have we had ? I will refer to the statement! made by the hon. leader of the government a little later on, hut we have had a statement from tiie hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), and if the fitness of the administration of the government of this country is to be measured by the utterances of that hon. minister upon this great occasion, I must say that the people of Canada will not form a very high estimate of our present administration. Why, a weak defence is worse than none. And if this was not a weak defence, if it was not pitiably destitute of argument:, then I must be singularly unable to appreciat'e the statement of the hon. gentleman. But his remarks have gone into cold print and the country will be able to estimate them at what they are worth. The hon. gentleman asks would the English workingmen be favourably disposed to Canada, if Canada
was the means of increasing the price of food in Great Britain. But these hon. gentlemen opposite were teaching us during eighteen years they were In opposition-true they have dropped it pretty well in the last four or five years since they have got into power-but during eighteen years previous they kept telling us that the consumer pays the duty. Well, what do we propose ? We propose that such a duty should be placed upon foreign goods by Great Britain as would exclude from the British market foreign products and allow Canadian products to enter free. What then will the British artisan and workman buy V He will buy the produce of the Canadian farm, and he will buy it free of duty. So that it is most idle for the hon. gentleman to advance that argument, because the argument inevitably defeats itself.
But he says, as an argument to support, if he can, this frail and tottering edifice of a one-sided preference, that it was a step towards Imperial unity. Sir, words in favour of Imperial unity do not come very well from my hon. friend. What progress is the government making in the direction of Imperial unity when they send back that de-sp- T'-hich, prematurely and unwisely as I say. refuses to discuss the question of Imperial defence and the unity of the empire. In what regard will the hon. Minister of Agriculture tell us are they advancing Imperial unity when they utterly refuse to even consider the question of Imperial defence ? He also tells ns-and it is a pity that these hon. gentlemen cannot have a little more consideration for our home affairs and not travel so far afield-that Sir Michael Hicks-Beneli missed the chance of his life when he introduced tiie change in his tariff and did not declare (without being asked and without being solicited, of course) that he would take off entirely the duty from the produce of Canada. When such a statement is made. I would like to ask the right hon. premier and the members of the government if they were taken by surprise when that change was made in the British tariff ? Did not they know that that change was to he brought about ? Were they the only people in the whole civilized world who did not realize that that change was coming ? Why, I, as one of the youngest members of this House and the most modest, told them what was coming, told them that Great Britain would have to change its trade policy and that the stability of the British Empire depended upon the conbined policy of Great Britain and her colonies with regard to trade. In speaking thus, I was not speaking on my own authority, but on the authority of the greatest of British statesmen, Mr. Chamberlain, who said : If you ask me what will be the destiny of Great Britain for the future. I answer that it will depend on the attitude taken by the great colonies of Great Britain. When all the world knew that this change was to be brought about, I must assume that this government was not

altogether asleep and that they knew something about it. But. if they did know about it, what did they do before that policy was announced to secure a preference for Canada in Great Britain such as the Minister of Agriculture says Sir Michael Hieks-Beach should have inaugurated at that time ? I say that a more completely condemnatory statement could not have been made by the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite then was made by the premier's own lieutenant, the Minister of Agriculture. Except that it introduces something that I wish to lead up to. I need hardly trouble very much about the speech of the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). He wanders from post to pillar, but he always comes back to his first love. He gave ns a very nice review of many steps in the history of Canada. jT do not think he went back quite to the visit of Columbus, but he did go over most of the important steps in the history of the country for the last fifty years. And it is significant that every one of these steps was a step marking the progress of the Conservative party.
And he opposed them.

Yes, those steps were opposed by the hon. gentlemen who are now in and of the government. And the hon. gentleman (Mr. Charlton) tells us- and it is a very nice moral sentiment-that the only great thing to consider is what is best in the interests of Canada, and that tiiis should be our guiding star. That comes well indeed from the hon. member for North Norkolk. who. according to his own declaration in this House-and I am sorry he is not present-though lie knew in lS7(i. 1877 and 187.8 that the true policy for Canada was the protective policy advocated by Sir John Macdonald, yet, in company with the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) for eighteen years-aye, for twenty-five years and more-kept his mouth shut, so far as saying a word in favour of that policy. On the contrary, he went up and down the country denouncing the policy which he knew to be in the best interests of Canada. And yet lie comes here to give us a moral lesson and tell us what to do in the best interests of the Dominion. Of course he is supported by the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Fraser) who speaks of him as the gentleman who is responsible for ' the sanctity of the Sabbath and the chastity of the home.' But 1 object to these bon. gentlemen giving us moral advice. I object at least, to taking it. until, as tlie hon. member for Victoria suggests. 1 find that their conduct is consistent with their utterances. Now, tdie lion, gentleman (Mr. Charlton) says that there will probably be many wars in which Canada will not be concerned. I do not join witli him in that view. I contend that the position we must take in this colony is that Whatever war affects

Great Britain, must affect us. Our destiny is inseparably bound up with that of Great Britain and I thank God it is so ; for that is where I want my destiny to be. We bear of. ' Little Englanders.' Let us not have any narrow Canadians who think there can be prosperity for Canada when the prestige of Great Britain begins to decline. I believe that prestige never will decline, but that, with the unity of the empire,.of which the Minister of Agriculture speaks so eloquently. Great Britain, witli her colonies surrounding her, will go on and prosper, and. in years to come, will become greater and grander than she has ever been in the past.
Now, the hon. member for North Norfolk has given us advice. He says it is to be a go-as-you-please affair, that we are just to give what we like, and therefore Britain is not to count on anything. What would the hon. gentleman say if. in the case of Canada being attacked by tlie United States Britain were to say, Ob. you need not count on our defence, you need not be sure we will defend you with men or arms or ships. But what Britain says, and what Britain has verified, is this : In the remotest part of our dependencies, whenever a British subject is attacked, the whole strength of the British army will be put forth in liis defence, in vindication of British justice and British rights. That is tlie position that we have to reciprocate. It is not a question of money alone, but it is a question of the enemies of Britain knowing that the whole empire is united as one man for tlie defence of every part of it.
Now, the member for North Norfolk says we may run up against the Munroe doctrine. Sir, I think it is unfortunate that matters of this kind should be aired in this way in the parliament of a British country! The hon. gentleman was discussing a proposal to formulate a scheme of universal defence of the empire, and he says if we do that we may run up against tlie Munroe doctrine. Now what position are we in ? Hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem to understand the proposition. The premier and his colleagues are going to Britain where they want something in tlie nature of a contribution to a defence fund from every colony of tile empire, some basis agreed upon by which each part of the empire will voluntarily contribute for the pur-p se of raising a defence fund available for tlie whole empire. It has nothing to jlo with the wars of Britain in Europe, but it is a proposition that each part of the whole shall contribute voluntarily to a fund for the defence of the empire. Yet when it is proposed to do this the hon.member for North Norfolk says we will run up against the Monroe doctrine: Has it come to this, that with all the strength of the empire, united as it would be if any part were attacked, we are to live in fear and trembling of tlie Monroe doctrine? In the first place, I have no faith in tlie hon. gentleman's argument; in the second place. I am not prepared to take

[DOT]4762
that cowardly attitude, even if I believed in the suggestion of the bon. gentleman.
Now I come to what is. after all, of more interest to the country, and that is the attitude taken by the hon. gentleman who leads this government. He began his speecli with what I may call a left-handed compliment to the leader of the opposition. 1 think he was not as generous as he might have been, I think he was not as just as lie might have been. I think it hardly did credit to the accustomed politeness of the leader of the government. I.et me make a comparison. I may be a little partial, I may not lie the best judge, but 1 have endeavoured to listen dispassionately to the arguments that have been advanced, and I would like to have some unprejudiced person who lias listened to the magnificent argument-I would call it so if the hon. gentleman himself was not present-presented by the leader of the opposition, and contrast it witli the speech of any member of the government, or any supporter of the government delivered to-night upon this question. I acknowledge that in some lines of eloquence I do not think I will be speaking disparagingly of our honoured leader if I say he does not hold a candle to the leader of the government. I am told, and I believe the story is true, that among the very numerous admirers of the leader of the government, a countryman of his own came here from a long distance down in the province of Quebec, to hear the hon. gentleman speak. After listening to him in rapt attention, he went out. and was asked what he thought of the Prime Minister, and he said : ' Sir Wilfrid Laurier, he speak long. Sir Wilfrid I.aurier, he speak well. Sir Wilfrid I.aurier, he say nothing.'
Oh, oh.
Hon. gentlemen may say oh just as much as they like, but we will have the judgment of the country upon this question.
You had that before.

Yes, but that is not the final judgment, as hon. gentlemen know. They pretend to be very happy for the present, and some hon. gentlemen who look very happy are not so. I see one hon. gentleman who is trying to smile, and his smile has just about as much relation to mirth as the grin of a jackass eating thistles. Now, I was going to say that when the leader of this government discussed this question to-night he failed to rise to its importance. and avoided it at almost every point. Although the little incident that I have related was perhaps somewhat exaggerated in expression, still we know that in the matter of talking without committing himself to anything definite, the hon. leader of the government transcendentl.v surpasses anybody upon either side of the House. We are told by the leader of the
government that the suggestion put forward by the leader of the opposition, although good in substance, comes too late, that we have waited too long. What has the government done in that regard ? Is it not their duty rather than the duty of the opposition to formulate a policy in this matter, to take the country into their confidence, and to ascertain the opinion of the country as a guide to the Prime Minister and his colleagues when they go to that conference ? They would then be in a far better position to make suggestions to the other gentlemen appearing at that conference than they will be under present circumstances.
Now, although the conduct of the government has been marked by conspicuous silence in regard to many great questions that have been suggested on this side of the House, although the government have adopted a hesitating, vacillating policy in many cases where it would have been well that they should have declared themselves, yet in this one point I charge that silence would have been golden and that it would have been more prudent, and statesmanlike, if the government were not able to agree in that measure of Imperial defence to have kept quiet, at all events, at that juncture upon this point. There was no necessity- for making a declaration upon the matter one way or the other. It was at a time when the South African war was still raging and it was all important that in the eyes of the world Great Britain should be seen with her colonies rallied around her and that there should be no suggestion that they were faltering in their defence. Therefore, I charge that it was weak, unwise and unstatesmanlike on the part of the right hon. leader of the government and his cabinet to send that message to Great Britain at the time. It has had a bad effect in Australia. Mr. Chamberlain said that the Australian Commonwealth was following in the wake of Canada, that Canada had set the example and that as Canada was the stepping stone, the Commonwealth of Australia was in that way a stepping stone toward the greater unity of the British Empire. But we are setting a bad example this time. The example of the right hon. gentleman is an incentive to the premier of Australia and he has announced his antagonism to the scheme. What is the principle which he announces ? He announces that they will have an independent defence, that they will defend their own commonwealth. Hoes Canada want to take that attitude ? Canada cannot take that attitude and there is no destiny for Canada as a British colony except she accepts some reasonable scheme for the general defence of the empire.
The right hon. leader of the government, when in London, told the people of Great Britain that Canada gave this preference out of generosity and out of a sense of appreciation of the many obligations that Can-

a da was under to Great Britain. In Toronto, as lias been pointed out, lie takes a different jiosition and it is bad enough when these two speeches conflict with each other. But the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) is again an unwise friend in coming to the defence of the government, like the lion. Minister of Agriculture ujOH. Mr. Fisher), because he brings confusion to the ranks. He contends that Canada owes nothing to Great Britain that with the consumption of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Canada wiped out every obligation that she owed to Great Britain for protection in the past. Which of these hon. gentlemen is right ? But. the right hon. gentleman said in London that we wanted nothing and that he was ready to give this preference as a free gift. That is not the position that Mr. Chamberlain takes in regard to the same matter. Mr. Chamberlain, I think, hon. gentlemen opposite will admit, is a practical statesman, and in discussing this very matter of closer trade relations and closer relations generally between Great Britain and her colonies, and particularly Canada, he said :
But my first point is that in the proposal and the suggestion which has hitherto been made there is no sufficient quid pro quo, the advantage offered is not enough to induce this country to take the certain loss and the possible risk which would be involved in revising altogether its present commercial policy.
In other words, Mr. Chamberlain takes the only statesmanlike attitude that can be taken when he says :	When I represent
my own goods I can be generous, but when I represent the people of Great Britain I can only be just. AVhen I give anything I must have a quid pro quo. That is the position that the statesmen of Canada must take if they wish to meet the views or the people of Canada.

Dredging-Dredge vessels, repairs, Manitoba,

How many dredges nave you in Manitoba now ?
The MINISTER Or PUBLIC WORKS. Two. There is the old dredge at Winnipeg and the tug Sir Hector which are in need of repairs.
Where is this dredging going to be done ?
The dredging that is going on now is at the mouth of the Red river, between the Red river and Lake Winnipeg.
Is there to be any dredging to be done this year at Sault Ste. Marie ?

Yes. We have asked for tenders which we Mr. LENNOX.
have received but I have not disposed of them as yet.
What amount will be spent in dredging there ?
I cannot say, but there is a large amount of work to be done there.

I do not know if the minister is fully aware that there is a great need of dredging there. I have been there quite recently and I can testify to the fact that while we have on the Canadian side a canal in certain respects superior to the American canal there is a very serious defect in the approaches to the Canadian side. They have asked for dredging there frequently and although that dredging is extremely urgent it has not been attended to during the last three years. I may add that there are no docking facilities at Sault St. Marie. There is a government dock but the water is so low that large steamers cannot come up to it, and in fact the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers are obliged to resort to the American channel. Although Sault Ste. Marie is the twelfth port of entry in the Dominion, yet the custom house is kept in a leased building, and the post office is quite out of proportion to the importance of the place. When I say that 2S,000,000 tons a year pass through the Sault canal; 20,000,000 tons more than through the Suez canal and that the facilities on the Canadian canal are inferior to those on the American canal, it will be recognized that is a humiliating condition of things which calls for immediate remedy. I would urge upon the Minister of Public Works to improve the approaches to the Canadian canal and also the docking facilities.

I concur in what the hon. gentleman has said. There is not enough water on the Canadian side and our ships are obliged to go on the other side. I was there a year ag'o and I know that. I appreciate it to such an extent that we have this year in the estimates a pretty large sum of money to go on with the work. As to the public buildings I may tell my bon. friend that we have also "in the estimates a sum to provide for them and a site has been bought. We have therefore looked after the interest of that town, much more than the hon. gentleman would think.
What is the amount voted for dredging ?

I do not pretend to be an expert, but from information I have gathered, I should think that $25,000 will scarcely do anything towards the improvements which I have mentioned. I under-

stand that the necessary dredging to prevent the humiliating spectacle of Canadian ships having to use the American canal would cost about $300,000.

I am very glad that one of the leaders of the opposition has at last gone to Sault Ste. Marie. I may repeat here what I said elsewhere :	Wait till next year, and when I
ask for money then I will not be accused by the opposition of spending too much. I know I am not asking enough to carry on - the whole work, but I believe I have asked enough to give a contract that will be completed in another year.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) has just come from Sault Ste. Marie having been up there with the leader of the opposition in the province of Ontario, and I apprehend that he has learned considerable of the existing conditions. I quite agree with him that the government needs to expend a very considerable sum of money in deepening the channel to the Canadian lock, but I would like the hon. gentleman to understand that for many years that lock was existing as it is now under a Conservative government and they never even thought of appropriating any money to deepen the channel. You can search in vain through ' Hansard ' for a suggestion from a Conservative member up to the present date, that money should be expended in deepening the Canadian channel. The Canadian lock was built under a Conservative government, and as any engineer will admit the channel was defective originally and is defective now. This government is spending money to deepen the channel so as to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway boats and all other boats to navigate through the Canadian channel. The Canadian Pacific Railway boats never have gone there, not because of there not being sufficient water but because of the fact that they get their supplies from the American side. There is water enough for them to go through the Canadian channel, but they go to the American lock because they get their supplies there, and if the hon. gentleman had not been quite so anxious to make a point in the interest of the Conservative party in the province he would have endeavoured to understand the exact situation. I know the situation and I know that there is water enough on the Canadian side for the large boats to navigate the Canadian lock.
And to reach the wharfs.

There is really no use of their reaching the wharfs because there is nothing there at present for them. But the Canadian Sault is growing. We hear just to-day that Mr. Clergue is turning out steel rails and he is doing that by reason of the
bonus granted and the vim that has been put into that country on account of the concessions granted by the Liberal government in the province of Ontario. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) wants to make any political capital out of the situation we are prepared to argue that point out with him. Perhaps this is not the place to do it, but whatever credit there is for giving a channel for safe navigation through the Canadian lock is due to the present Liberal government which is providing the money to do the work there. The Conservative government never did that when they were in power.

1 am bound to say that 1 do not look upon this question as a question of politics, and I do not wish to make a point against this government or for the Conservative party. I consider that a man who has the honour of a seat in this House and who visits the country and finds things that he thinks might be improved upon, is bound to mention these things in the proper place. As to the information which my hon. friend has vouchsafed to me and the House to-night, I have been only two days in Sault Ste. Marie, and I am sure that his information is very defective. I would take, for instance, the point raised by my hon. friend that the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers do not come to the Canadiau side because they get their supplies on the American side. That may be so; but it is absolutely contrary to the information given to me there by competent men, far more competent than my hon. friend, and knowing a great deal more than he does about the subject. As to the suggestion that they wished to make a point against this government, I can assure the hon. Minister of Public Works that such an idea did not enter their minds. As a matter of fact, the reason given by business men in the Sault why the Canadian Pacific Railway steamers got their supplies on the American side was that they could not come to the Canadian side. It is true, the lock there was built by the Conservative government, but it is in the right place. Nobody complains of the location of the lock, and in some respects it is far better than the American lock. It moves much more quickly, and is therefore sought by men who want to get their vessels through quickly; but I believe this government finished that lock.
No. The Conservative government gave Messrs. Ryan & Haney $90,OCX) to finish the lock before their time.
That may be. At any rate, it was finished about the time there was a change of government.
Before that.

However, what is retarding progress there is the need of dredging on a considerable scale. Competent men told me that it was a matter of somej $400,000.

The figure surprised me, and probably the dredging could be done for u less sum; but there Is no doubt that it will require a far greater amount than the amount mentioned by the minister, to place that port on a proper tooting. On the American side they have all the conveniences and facilities that are required, and the vessels go there preferably to coming to our side. On our side there is a wharf, but the water near it is not deep enough for large vessels.
Two wharfs.

There is oidy one government wharf. The other wharf was built by private enterprise. I think it is right, irrespective of politics, for si man who knows these facts and has visited the place, to rise in his seat in this House and mention them without being criticised in the small picayune spirit the hon. gentleman has shown.

Not carried by any means. I want you to understand, Mr. Chairman, that I am on my feet, and until I sit down it is not carried. I can talk on that question as welL as on any other, and I am not going to be put down in that way. I understand that there are two dredges in Manitoba, but I am told that they, are not very suitable for the dredging to be done. I understand that one is engaged at the St. Andrew's rapids. Is this merely for r<;-pairing the old dredge, or is the purpose to build another for the work there ?

The sum of money 1 am asking is to make repairs to the old dredge, which is doing Mr. MONK.
fairly good work, but which needs to be put in better shape. The next item is to provide a new dredge. That will make three.
Dredging-Man., self-propelling snag boat,
Is that the beginning of the new dredge '-because $10,000 is a small amount to put on a dredge.

This $10,000 is to build a snag boat, similar to what the Americans have on the Red river on their side. These snag boats are not expensive. I think with these three dredges we shall have all we require to do the work.

Before this item passes 1 wish to thank the hon. Minister of Public Works for the action he has taken this year in assisting the people who own boats on the Assiniboine and Red rivers. The dredge which was built in 1881 and is now to be repaired has been used to dredge out the mouth of the Red river where it empties into Lake Winnipeg. The dredge is entirely out of repair, and it was running last year at great loss. It is not being, used in St. Andrew's rapids, but at the mouth of the river. The necessity of renewing the dredge has been brought before the minister for the last two or three years, and I beg to thank him for taking the matter up in a thoroughly businesslike manner. I said some time ago that I thought the word Manitoba was never mentioned in this House by the lion. Minister of Public Works -that he had apparently forgotten it. I wish to take back that statement. With regard to the snag boat, I may say that in the Red river, both above and below the St. Andrew's rapids there are many boulders and sunken logs, so that vessels cannot navigate the river. The steamer ' Gertie PI.' went up the river, and has been niue days above the rapids, and cannot get back owing to tlie boulders and snags in the way. 1 was at a meeting last fall of the board of trade which is composed largely of friends of hon. gentlemen opposite-in fact almost entirely. A very large deputation came to that board, and the board very strongly recommended that a dredge be purchased to remove those boulders and other impediments in the river. I am sure that the board of trade, composed of gentlemen on both sides of politics, as well as the citizens of Winnipeg, generally, will thank the hon. Minister of rublic Works for having put these sums in the estimates.
Is this the full cost of the dredge ?
Yes.
When will it be available for work ?
Next season.
Where are you building it ?
Probably on Lake Winnipeg.
Are you building it by contract ?

I do not know yet. I will take the best means.
Bryon Island to Anticosti, cable, &c., connection, $25,000.
Will the hon. minister explain this item of $25,000 ?

My hon. friend perhaps will allow me to lay on the Table a map, which will make the whole thing clear to those who take an interest in the question. I want to connect Anticosti Island, which is connected with our north shore, with the Magdalen Islands, which are connected with Cape Breton. Then we will have a complete connection with the cable at Canso and Sydney and a complete Canadian telegraphic system on Canadian shore.
What is the object of the cable to Anticosti ?

Anticosti Island is connected with the north shore by a cable telegraph system on the north shore. We have reached St. Paul's Bay, and my idea is that we should have a complete system of telegraphs on our own soil, and my ambition is to take that system of telegraphs to Montreal as soon ns possible. To reach Quebec it would cost about $13,000 to $15,000 because we have already a telegraph system at Grosse Isle. I do not see why, now that we expect the Marconi system will work well, we should not have a telegraph system of our own instead of relying on New York for our commercial news. Montreal and Toronto should be made, and will be made, Canadian centres of distribution for all news, commercial and other. When I have completed those lines to Sydney and Canso our Canadian telegraph system will have communication with all the cables, American, English and French. We have only a very small sum to spend this year to have that complete telegraph system.

Are these cables open to use by the public ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC AArORKS. Yes, it is a regular telegraph system.
For extBnsion of the Magdalen Islands telegraph system to Bryon Island by means of submarine cable, $9,000.

What is the distance from Magdalen to Bryon Island ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC AArORKS. 14 knots. From Anticosti to the north shore, 104 knots.
Any tenders asked ?

No, we have had a cable ship. We are asking quotations in Germany and England for cables and wires. We have cabled the best firms in England and Germany, and as we have a cable ship ready, we will do the work ourselves.
Mabou to Port Ha'vkesbury, $5,600.
Is there any telegraph line between these points now ?

Yes, we are in the hands of the Anglo-American Company, which I want to get rid of.
St. Peter's to Louisbourg and Scatari Island- extension, Gabarus to North Sydney, $4,900.
I suppose the same is true in this case-there is already a telegraph line there ?
No, there is none. We want to reach the lighthouse there, which is now isolated.
Surely there is telegraphic communication between Louisbourg and St. Peter's ?
I was speaking of Scatari Island, to which there is no communication. My deputy tells me there is a line of telegraph along the railway from St. Peter's to Louisbourg, but there is none on the coast.
But a person in St. Peter's can telegraph to another in Louisbourg ? The object of this vote must be to establish a system of government telegraphs throughout the country ?

It is surely a beginning in that part of the country. But my main object is to have direct communication with the cables at Sydney and Canso, and then take the system up to the city of Montreal, and-well, further up if the country desires.
It seems to be a quiet way of undermining the Postmaster General.
Oh, no, the Postmaster General is too strong for that.

Well, perhaps not completely undermining him, but undermining him so far as this telegraph service is concerned. How many miles of this telegraph open for the use of the public service does the government now own outside of the Yukon ?	.
Outside of the Yukon we have about 4,400 miles. AVith these extensions we shall have about 4,700 miles, and, in the Yukon 2,135 miles.

Is there auy substantial revenue from these lines ?
The MINISTER OF I>UBLIC WORKS. Yes, that will be found in my report. I may say, in passing, that the Yukon line is doing very well. The revenue for April was about $11,500.
After deducting expenses, or gross ?
Gross.
Did the minister ascertain, according to the understanding of some days ago, what portion of the business on the Yukon line was government business ?

During March, the departmental telegrams amounted to about $1,100. I suppose it will run about $1,000 a month. If lion, gentlemen will refer to my report, page 11 of the telegraph report, they will see that the revenue last year outside of the Yukon was about $15,000, and the expenditure about $60,000.. I may explain that when these lines are completed we hope to do better. And the House must not lose sight of the fact that these lines are built where private companies would not build them. Take, for instance, the North Shore line-there is no appreciable revenue from it, and no company would build a line there.
Aside from the cost of building, it cost $60,000 to run these telegraphs, and the revenue was $15,000. That revenue included government business, I suppose ?

Yes, but we do scarcely any business except on the Yukon line. But, as I say, all the lines have been built where private companies would not build them. The North Shore line, for instance, was built in the interest of navigation and trade.

So far as the construction of lines between points already served by lines owned by private companies is concerned, it does not seem to me that it is justifiable unless the government is preparing to establish a system of government telegraphs throughout the country. I cannot see any other principle, upon which it can be justifiable. It must be very much more expensive to the country to construct a line for its own use than to pay for the amount of business usually done at the regular prices of the established lines. Perhaps I may be mistaken in my deductions, but that is what I would suppose. So I can only regard this as the initiation of a system of government telegraphs throughout the country. Is that the policy?
I would not say more than I have already

said. I have not been authorized by my colleagues to say more. My object in asking for this money is to connect our system with the different cables at Sydney and Canso. We have given $80,000 to the Marconi Company to establish a station in Cape Breton. If that system works well, we shall have a means of communicating with the other side of the ocean besides the cable. But we shall have also the cable to rely upon. Speaking for myself, I believe that the cable will be, for some time to come, the safest means of communicating. I hope that Mr. Marconi will be able more and more to improve his system. We have tested it, and are testing it every day between Belle Isle and the North Shore. There are two stations in charge of my department. When the atmosphere is dry and the conditions favourable, the system works well; but when the atmosphere is damp and high winds prevail, it does not work well. It is a very difficult thing to maintain regular communications between the two stations when the conditions are unfavourable. The distance between Belle Isle and the North Shore is twenty-two miles.

Are not many of these points where the hon. gentleman now proposes to build cables, points well suited for working the Marconi system, assuming that system can be effectively worked, and if so, would it not be better to learn whether that system would be practicable before expending so large an amount of money in the construction of a cable ? For example, between Louisbourg and Seatari, if I remember the geographical conditions accurately, I would suppose that would be a proper place for the establishment of this system.

Yes, but it is so unsafe now I would not trust it for commercial purposes. It works when the weather is fine, and it does not work when the weather is damp. On different occasions last winter I asked news from our agents, and they answered that the instrument was sticking. I may say that we have not the best receivers, although they have been installed by Mr. Marconi's agents. Mr. Marconi told me these receivers were not the best. Since then we have put in new receivers, and I understand with better results. But I am quite sure the cables will be required for service for some time to come.

I would like to know whether the minister has taken hold of this Marconi system merely as an experiment, or whether he found out before taking hold of it that it would be of some practical use. From his last remarks I would infer that he does not know whether this $80,000 is going to be of any substantial benefit to the Dominion. If stations are to be established

at Glace Bay for communication across the Atlantic, I cannot understand why we are establishing cable lines along very much shorter distances, from Anticosti to the Magdalen islands, and from Scatari to Louisbourg. I cannot understand how it is going to operate across the Atlantic when it will not operate between nearer points. I . would like to know whether the government is going to establish an experimental station to aid people in scientific investigations, or is he going into this large expenditure to save money to the government on submarine cables ? If that is the case, I would suggest that a very suitable point for the development of the system for a short distance would be from Gape Tormentine to Cape Traverse, where people are suffering a gross injustice by reason of an ineffective service by submarine cable operated unjustly by a private company.

As the minister of telegraphs I arranged for the establishment of two Marconi systems last fall. I thought it was only fair to try it, as it did not cost much. We are paying a royalty of $500 a year for these two stations between the North Shore and Belle Isle. The station at Glace Bay is a government station. I am asking nothing for it in my estimates. It is a government question altogether, so much so that it is not placed in my estimates as Minister of Public Works and of Telegraphs. I am responsible for the establishment of that station, of course, but I did not make a bargain myself. I hope the Marconi system will be worked between ocean and ocean. But I say again that, after lia\ ing read a good many things that have been written on ,..e Marconi system and all the other wireless systems, I have come to the conclusion that it will take some years before these wireless systems can be worked safely for commercial purposes. Mr. Marconi and others are all the time improving their system, but I am afraid no country will rely on these wireless systems. I would rather rely for safe communication on cables that I know and have tested. Still, the Marconi, the Slaby and other systems are making great progress.

The curious feature of the Situation seems to me that we are spending about $70,000 here in cables for short distances which certainly could be supplied by the Marconi system much more easily, if that system can be established across the Atlantic. The Marconi system has either arrived at a stage ai. which it is likely to be in some measure successful or it has not. Most people think it has, the government evidently thinks that it has, because they are voting $80,000 for the purpose of assisting that gentleman and his system. It certainly has been successful in England over much greater distances than those covered by some of 150$
these cables, if we are to believe all we read in the public press. It has been established over distances very much longer than between Louisbourg and Scatari.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WOlLvo. In all kinds of weather ?
So I understood.
I say no, I am sure of that.

Then he should not have permitted this sum of $80,000 to be put in the estimates for the purpose of cabling across the Atlantic. He seems to want to relieve himself from the responsibility for that particular vote. If it can be used at all in all weathers and under all conditions for any distance, then it certainly can be used between Louisbourg and Seat-terie. How far is it between these two points ?
About three or four miles.
About 15 miles.
From Louisbourg to Scatterie ?
From Louisbourg to Scatterie is about 15 miles.
That is what I would have supposed.
That is by land, but the channel is not more than three or four miles across.
Not that much.
Surely, if this system can be used for a distance of that kind, would it not be the proper course to delay proceedings a little before spending a great deal of money on these cables ?

The experience that I have had of the Marconi system between the North Shore and Belle Isle is such that I would not like to tell the commercial community that they could rely at all times on it. Last winter I asked for reports between the North Shore and Belle Isle, and I could not get them. This system works well in a dry temperature; that is our own experience. But Marconi and other scientists are working on the wireless system and improving it every day. There is no doubt that Marconi has been ahead of everybody else, but I would not take the responsibility of saying that the commercial community couid rely upon the wireless system at ail times and that is the reason why we have these cables.
You want to doubletrack the system.
