speechtext: We have an item, No. 92, which deals with this question.

I think the discussion is perfectly regular. We are considering whether or not we will spend money on cables. It is a perfectly proper thing to consider this matter and to point out that this expenditure may be unnecessary because you can have communication by means of the Marconi system. I do not think the discussion has gone beyond the range of what is proper on this item.
This $80,000 will be all.
How many instruments have you ?
As to that I do not know.
If it is regular, I might ns well find out whether you expect to use this system to communicate with the other side of the Atlantic.

The instruments which the hon. Minister of Public Works holds have no relation to the Mar-Mr. LEFURGEY.
coni contract. These were obtained before we made the Marconi contract. The contract simply is that we shall expend $80,000 to aid Mr. Marconi in putting up a station in the hope that it will be a success. If It is a failure we have specu-. lated in science and have not got much for our money, but if it is a success we gain by the fact that the Atlantic rates are to be decreased.
And you have the instruments besides, which you have bought ?

These instruments bought by the Public Works Department are outside the contract. The contract-also provides that for our own purposes we shall be able to get the instruments at cost price free from royalty, but the hon. Minister of Public Works had purchased these instruments before Mr. Marconi came here.
The instruments that are under my care cost $2,000.
You do not know how many you have ?
I have two stations under my care.
Did they cost $2,000 apiece ?
No, $2,000 for the two stations. We have one at Belle Isle and one on the north shore. This summer we will give them a fair trial and I think they will work well.
It does seem a pity that before laying this cable you had not made a fair trial with this system.
My own personal conviction is, that, useful as the wireless system may be, cables will always be necessary.
If cables will always be necessary, would it not be the part of wisdom to allow Mr. Marconi to go on with his experimenting and risk the cables until such time as he has perfected the system '!
The Governor in Council has decided otherwise.
The Minister of Public Works dissenting.
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works if the arrangement made with Mr. Marconi includes any improvements made in the future on the system ?

As far as the Department of Public Works is concerned, I am perfectly free to make any other arrangement with any other company. I have only instruments for two sta-

tions. If they work well I will be very thankful indeed. If they do not I will change them. I have not paid much for them. As to the hon. gentleman's question, the government have made their experiment and, as the lion. Minister of Finance says, if it works well we will have the bene-fitj and if it does not, we will lose.
That is not the question I wished to ask at all. I wished to know if any future improvements on the Marconi system were Included in the present arrangement ?

We pay 880,000 towards the construction of these stations, which will be completed, I expect within a few weeks or a few months. Be-vond that the Marconi Company stipulate that they will give us the instruments for the purposes of our lighthouse service and for the purposes of navigation, &c., but not for commercial purposes, and that will naturally include improvements at fair prices and without royalties. Anything of that kind which we require they must supply at a fair price without regard to royalty.
I thought you said we got it for nothing.
It means that we get them at manufacturer's prices without any cost for royalty. They must not charge us for royalty which is the chief cost in those things.
Have you purchased the future improvements that might be made in the Marconi system ?
I would not say that. [DOT]
Will the minister tell us the position exactly that we are in ?

Our main contract had relation to the creation of this station, and the other part was rather incidental to the arrangement and no great importance was attached to it. It provides whatever instruments we need for our lighthouses and for the safety of life and property, but not for general commercial purposes. we are entitled to get at a fair price without having to pay a royalty.

Then we are absolutely in the hands of the Marconi Company as regards any improvements they may make upon their system, and after this expenditure of $80,000 we will still have to pay the piper for any improvements they may make.

The Minister of Justice has sent for the contract and it will speak for Itself. We are paying the $80,000 mainly for the station, and Marconi will be interested in making his system as perfect ns possible. We are getting the benefit in the shape of reduced rates which
is the only way we get our compensation. The Minister of Justice thinks the word ' improvement ' is mentioned in the contract.
It appears that we are in a rather precarious position in regard to this matter. We have the Minister of rub-lie Works saying that he has no faith in the system.
I did not say that.

Well, he says that he has no absolute faith in the system. We are spending therefore $80,000 merely on an experiment, and I do not think we are justified tn paying $80,000 out of the public funds to assist an experiment on behalf of any person. The minister himself says that he is not sure that it can be used over a space of ten miles. If we are not entitled to the improvements which may be made in the Marconi system, our money is absolutely wasted and we are simply putting ourselves in the hands of any speculator that may come along.

I differ from my hon. friend as to the experiment, because I believe that whether it succeeds or fails it was a good thing for us to take hold of Marconi and give him a helping hand in a matter which was attracting world wide interest. Whether it succeeds or fails there is no question but that the public opinion of Canada has fully justified the government in taking the step it did. If it succeeds we will get our compensation in the shape of a ten cent rate instead of a twenty-five cent rate, and that is worth risking something for. Like Mark Twain's uncle who took the pork contract, we will be serving our country and making a nice thing out of it.
Has the minister a written report about those cables from Mr. Keeley ?
We have estimates.
Prepared by Mr. Keeley ?
Certainly.

I differ from the Min-ter of Finance, for I do not believe that the government of Canada should set itself up as an experimental station of any sort. Scientific investigations have gone on in this world for a great many years and I do not know of any government having assisted mere experiments. There are experiments on flying machines and other things, and the first thing we know the Minister of Finance and his colleagues will be making experiments in this line. We can very well allow such experiments to be carried on by the parties interested, and when completed we can reap the advantage of them. I notice that the government has not yet taken up the experiment'of the fast line of steamers across

the Atlantic, which is a very desirable experiment for the government to make in the interest of the country, and on which $80,000 could be much more wisely spent than on this wireless telegraphy which the minister himself does not know will be a success.

At this point I think there ought to be an understanding. We are asked from time to time to vote large sums of money -for matters which members of parliament necessarily know very little about. The one difficulty in the Welland canal for a full sized canal boat drawing 14 feet of water, 2(55 feet long, carrying 75,000 or 80,000 bushels of grain, is that when the boat comes to a unuge pier, the pier being built in the centre of the canal, it forms an obstruction to the passage of a full sized canal boat. As the hon. gentleman well knows, eoery pivot pier is in the centre of the canal. There is 45 feet of navigation on each side of the pier. The locks are, it is true, only 45 feet in width, but here is the difficulty. When these large boats come to a bridge the current, which is of considerable rapidity in the canal now by reason of all the water powers that are taken from the canal, is split at the bridge pier. One of these boats has only about 10 to 12 inches of water under her keel, and it is somewhat difficult to manage, money is being voted now to deepen that level to some extent, making it a clean 16 feet. That is what they need to have, that is what the Welland aqueduct has, that was built under the administration of the hon. member for Lanark. When these big boats come to the centre piers the current" is split, and they have to turn out of their natural course, and may either go into the bank or strike a pier. That does not often happen, but it does sometimes, and the danger of its happening drives vessels away from the Welland canal. If it happens once to a boat it destroys that boat as a money-making commodity. They have to send off for tugs to straighten them around, and they will probably break a portion of the pier. It destroys the earning value of that cargo, and perhaps of every cargo that it will take through the canal that season. Moreover it cauues delay, and the charge of navigation by reason of that is so great that these boats will not pass tnrough the canal when the pier is in the centre. The Hamilton and North-western Navigation Company bought two boats from Glasgow, the ' Strathcona ' and the ' Donaeona,' full canal size, which navigated the canal last Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
summer. They had to take the boats off the canal and they absolutely refused to put them on again as long as these centre piers existed. His chief captain, Mr. Norcross, who comes from our section, captain of one of his biggest boats, was down here interviewing the government to get them to remove the centre piers. They appreciate the danger and Mr. Wolvin is willing to put on a line of ships if the government will take out the centre piers. The superintending engineer two years ago, I think it was, recommended to the department,*if I am rightly advised, to put a sum in the estimates to remove the centre piers.
